utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will try and be shorter than that. May I deal with the sentencing elements, and I have indicated to my learned friend, if I deal with it just very gently. In our -- very generally. There are two principal considerations in any sentence that we submit the Court should take into account. One, that first part should reflect the overall gravamen of the situation itself; and secondly, what I will call an element of deterrence. In this case, it is perfectly clear from the facts that have been alleged and the court are very familiar with that this was an appalling crime, and therefore we would submit that the following sentences are appropriate: With regard to Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivacanin, if they were committed for what I will call JCE 1 or JCE 3, we submit that the appropriate sentence is one of life imprisonment. With regard to Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivacanin in respect of individual modes of liability or responsibility, namely, ordering or aiding and abetting, we submit that life imprisonment is the appropriate sentence. For Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Sljivacanin, for 7(3), we submit that the failure to prevent such a large number of people being killed and/or persecuted it should be life in prison, and for failure to punish, there should be a period of 10 to 15 years. In respect of Mr. Radic, if he were convicted of JCE 1 or 3, we submit, even though his part is not as significant as the other two, life imprisonment. In relation to Mr. Radic, for again, individual modes of liability, in this instance only aiding and abetting, we submit that life imprisonment is also appropriate. However, when we come to 7(3), liability, there are certain subplots. The failure to prevent basically the TO, if in actual fact the Court find that they were subordinated to him, the appropriate sentence would be between 10 and 15 years. Failure to punish the TO, sentence of 8 to 10 years, and if the Court is not satisfied of the issue of subordination in relation to the TO itself, there are clearly three other JNA soldiers who were directly subordinated to him. We would submit that the period would be between 4 and 6 years. Mr. Radic, I believe, has been in custody I think just over three years. I would not seek to address the Court on any other issue in relation to sentencing. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. I will then give the floor to Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would like to apologise now given the number of people who make up the respective teams assisting us and the Prosecutor. I have not had the time or the ability to put together a presentation for my closing argument. I will be reading out all the relevant numbers, though, and I will be using the tab given to us by Mr. Moore. Your Honours, this closing argument has been conceived as a response to the Prosecutor's final brief and the Prosecutor's closing argument. I will be using references not mentioned in Mr. Mrksic's final brief. As for any others that have been mentioned, we shall merely be using the substance of information indicating that the facts were indeed different from what the OTP have pleaded. We could say that the objective of all the parties involved in this trial was to, after more than 15 years, contribute to shedding some light on the events that occurred between the 20th and the 21st of November, 1991, at the Ovcara farm near Vukovar. Although at the outset this may have seemed an easy task, it was by no means easy, partly because of the long time that has passed, leaving a question mark over the evidence given by witnesses in terms of their precision and reliability, and also because there is an abundance of relevant documents that have in the meantime disappeared or have remained beyond the reach of the parties involved in this trial. Unfortunately, this documentation that the Defence looked for so hard, such as the operations log of the Guards Motorised Brigade and the briefing book of the Guards Motorised Brigade would certainly have allowed us to achieve a more reliable construction of these events that occurred over 15 years ago, as well as the respective roles of all of the protagonists. It would certainly have allowed us to critically assess the evidence given by those involved, evidence which they, as witnesses, brought before this Court. Another problem which made this task even more arduous has been the absence of a number of important witnesses who have not appeared before the Trial Chamber because my learned friends from the OTP simply dropped them or indeed because any effort to have them appear has proved too complicated even once court orders have been issued. However, these documents that the Mrksic Defence looked for so hard, sometimes physically by rummaging through the archives and sometimes by requesting these documents through official state bodies, have not been found. In all likelihood, it could be addressed in more detail by witnesses who regrettably are no longer with us or witnesses dropped by my learned friend. However, despite all the peculiarities of this case, we can say that the initial hypothesis that a case which only concerns the territory of a small town and its surroundings, such as Vukovar, and a time frame of a single day and night will be swiftly and simply concluded, has proved erroneous. Instead of that, over the one and a half years of this trial, both parties have presented a large number of witnesses and exhibits which we assessed in our final brief and which we are assessing now. When assessing the evidence, at the end of this trial, the parties were compelled to go again through more than 16.000 pages of the transcript and over 880 exhibits in order to be able, in their final briefs, to point out to the Court the relevant portions, and by cross-referencing, try to show and prove what among all the evidence given by witnesses was truthful and what was not, as well as the reasons why certain witnesses should not be given credibility. Although, in this way, the Defence has refreshed its memory of everything that went on in this case as well as all the evidence, it was quite surprised by the way that our learned friend Mr. Moore addressed all these issues in his own final brief. While reading their final brief, it was difficult sometimes to ascertain how certain conclusions were drawn that are stated in the final brief, and sometimes invoking certain portions of transcript came down to invoking isolated portions of the transcript taken out of context might fit the Prosecutor's purpose. However, many of these portions, once set in their proper context, do suddenly look different in the context of a witness's overall evidence. Sometimes my learned friend used generic phrases in order to obscure a more focused version on the roles played by certain individuals in all these events. For example, in one part of his final brief, he uses names, surnames, ranks, and positions occupied by certain people in order to corroborate some of his submissions. In other portions, he just refers generically to all these as OG South or the Guards Motorised Brigade, in a bid to suggest that all of this is one and the same thing, although, throughout the trial, we have been successful in distinguishing between all these various entities and units. In fact, this goes so far that, as witness Bogdan Vujic likes to say, even the representatives of the Supreme Command such as Colonel Pavkovic and Colonel Terzic are placed within the very same framework of OG South, although he himself at page 23, paragraph 44 of the final brief, states explicitly that they were detached to the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade as liaison officers, which implies that they were not part of the command nor could they receive any orders whatsoever from the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade or indeed the command of OG South. Colonel Pavkovic and Colonel Terzic, even in the OTP's submission, had no command function to perform within the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade. On page 13691 of the transcript, Mr. Sljivacanin testified: "Regulations that were in force in the Yugoslav People's Army and at that time since Pavkovic came from the superior command, it is true that Mrksic was unable to issue any assessment to him -- assignment." Sorry. My learned friend, on page 23 of his own brief, claims that Colonel Mrksic issued orders to Colonel Pavkovic. He makes this claim based on Mr. Sljivacanin's evidence more specifically at page 13550. However, if we consider the response of Mr. Sljivacanin quoted above, it is clear that Colonel Mrksic could never have issued any orders whatsoever to Colonel Pavkovic, an officer belonging to the superior command and the supervisor of the command of Guards Motorised Brigade and OG South. Eventually this was confirm by all the relevant witnesses; not only all the relevant Defence witnesses but OTP witnesses as well. For example, the oft quoted witnesses Trifunovic, the relevant pages being 8064 and 8065. The following example could be found at page 26 of the OTP's final brief, where in paragraph 55 the submission is made that Colonel Mrksic resubordinate to the Petrova Gora TO to the 80th Motorised Brigade and the Leva Supoderica Detachment to the 12th corps by an order which was admitted in this trial as Exhibit 422. These submissions about the signing of that order and report also apply to Exhibit 386 dated the 21st of November, 1991. During the trial, it seemed quite obvious that the said order was not signed by Colonel Mrksic but, rather, by the then stand-in commander, chief of staff Miodrag Panic. The transcript reference is 14413, lines 21 through 25. "[In English] On the same statement, on page 58, did you state that that morning, the 21st of November, 1991, you signed an order on resubordinating these units as deputy commander in the absence of Mr. Mrksic? Did you say that? Do you remember that?" It was the question. "Answer: Yes, there is a document concerning that and I signed it. "Question: All right, Mr. Panic. Tell me, please, this order here you signed at 6 a.m. on the 21st of November, 1991 pursuant to the order of the 1st Military District 15 -- 115/151; correct? "Answer: Yes." This is transcript number 14414, lines 10 to 14. [Interpretation] Furthermore, it seemed indisputable to us that on the 21st of November, 1991, Colonel Mrksic was in Belgrade. If I understand my learned friend correctly, and if he is suggesting that it remains to be proved whether Colonel Mrksic left for Belgrade on the 20th of November, 1991, then in relation to the 21st of November no such statement was made. Despite this, in his final brief, he claims that Colonel Mrksic wrote and signed both the order and the report to his superior command, dated the 21st of November, 1991. We all know that this report was again compiled by his deputy, Miodrag Panic, who, at the time, was chief of staff. Yesterday, my learned friend yet again repeated this stunning claim in his closing argument, which moved me to conclude -- which led me to conclude that he is holding on to this story that Colonel Mrksic flew to Belgrade on the morning of the 21st of November, 1991, and not in a car on the 20th of November, 1991, because he is aware of the fact that until his departure there had been nothing at all to suggest that a tragedy would occur. Any information that eventually reached him at the meeting and the regular briefing, any information shared by Lieutenant Colonel Panic, as well as some information shared by Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, clearly indicated that an omission had been made in terms of security, but also that the situation was by no means critical and was now again fully under controlment. This is what witness Panic has to say about this. The transcript reference is 14328 and 14329. "[In English] Yes, yes. When I informed him about all of this, I said it wouldn't be a bad thing if some of the security organs or military police went to Ovcara to indicate certain things or offer assistance in professional terms if necessary to Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic. I don't know whether he sent anyone. I think he did, and I think on the basis of everything I remember and having made these previous statements too. I think that he actually did send some people there, and I think that Mile Bozic was among them. He was there in Negoslavci and at the command post or, rather, in a house there near the command post." [Interpretation] And this is what Witness Vojnovic says about it. The page reference is 8980, lines 18 through 23. "[In English] Question: You say Mrksic was angry and I told you don't even tell me about that. Yes, don't even tell me about that. Your report on Mrksic was in relation to the situation such that it was on the time you left the hangar at Ovcara. "Yes." On the transcript 18983, lines 13 to 23: "Question: You told him what had happen. You told him what was going on. POW had been attacked, you are leaving the hangar, you are on the way to the command. Some degree of order is now established because these people are now physically separated from the terror men; right? "Answer: Precisely. "Question: Could Colonel Mrksic have told you and other commanders perhaps no more than the following words: Don't even tell me about that, meaning, take any measures that you can with your units, the units at your disposal. If that proves out to be [indiscernible], I shall authorise that you use units from the military company of the 1st Military Company and the armoured vehicle to the chief of staff of the Operational Group. "The witness: No, I heard nothing like that." [Interpretation] There is evidence to suggest that before his departure from Belgrade that evening on the 20th of November, which is something addressed by Witness Gluscevic, but also Witness Panic, Lieutenant Colonel Panic, Mrksic warned everyone that there should be no such incidents, and he requested that the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, through the chief of staff Lieutenant Colonel Panic, in case of need, should be given reinforcements in order to allow him to secure the hangar. My learned friend, in this inappropriate way, is trying to hold up his -- his claim that on the 20th of November, the evening of the 20th of November, Colonel Mrksic was in fact in Negoslavci. We know for a fact that he wasn't there simply because a large number of witnesses confirmed this. On the other hand, even the OTP witness Trifunovic claims that Mrksic was not in Negoslavci that evening. However he claims that he was in Berak and that he return the next morning, which is not consistent with the truth, because it is beyond dispute that at 6.00 in the morning Lieutenant Colonel Panic, chief of staff, signed an order on Commander Mrksic's behalf which he could only have ever done if Mrksic had not been around. This story with the alleged order, which is on page 28 of the OTP final brief, about the appointment of Miroljub Vujic as TO commander and we need to remember that no one, save for Witness Trifunovic, ever claims to have seen this and the OTP gives the following transcript references 8210 and 8371, as opposed to pages 8285 and 8286 from the evidence given by the same witness, where Witness Trifunovic, of all people, claims that it is possible that this order was signed on the 21st of November, the morning of the 21st, which means precisely during Colonel Mrksic's absence from Negoslavci. In that case, the order could only have been signed by Lieutenant Colonel Panic, the chief of staff. However, there is nothing in the war log to suggest the existence of such an order, which leaves this as a mere fabrication on the part of Witness Trifunovic in a bid to please the OTP. This was eventually corroborated by Vujevic himself in a different trial in Belgrade last week. At page 136, paragraph 375 of his final brief, my learned friend himself claims that Dusan Jaksic was removed and Miroljub Vujevic appointed as TO commander of TO Vukovar by Major Veselin Sljivacanin. It is quite obvious that my learned friend cannot make up his mind, and what he would like best is for all of the accused to be responsible for everything. In the chapter about the evacuation of the hospital in Vukovar and the Zagreb Agreement, on pages 43 through 45 of the OTP final brief, the substance of what this agreement was really about is obscured. What is also obscured is the nature of the contacts between the ECMM and ICRC with military officials in Negoslavci and Vukovar. It is quite clear that the persons that the agreement spoke about were only the wounded and the sick and that the observers such as Kypr, Schou, and Cunningham held talks with officers from the SSNO, and the command of the 1st Military District who spoke on behalf of the Supreme Command, General Raseta and Admiral Brovet and not in fact with the OG South command. Exhibits 322, 333, and 344 clearly show this. Yesterday my learned friend, in part at least, interpreted Exhibit 320, which is the ECMM report indicating that an ICRC representative was thrown out of the hospital at 2000 hours on the 19th of November, which is not really true if one takes into account what that same representative sold Vesna Bosanac, which is something that Vesna Bosanac addressed at 686, lines 14 through 25. At any rate, we find the following sentence in that report, which is a sentence not quoted by my learned friend. "[In English] After receiving instructions from General Raseta, the registration process began and the sick and wounded were loaded into bus and ambulances." [Interpretation] On page 57, in paragraph 128, referring to the meeting between Cyrus Vance and Colonel Mrksic, my learned colleague states something which is not to be found in either Exhibit 418, nor was it uttered by the witness Trifunovic. In his talk with Mr. -- with Colonel Mrksic, Mr. Cyrus Vance was briefly informed of the situation in the field and with the activities of the OG South, but he neither expressed the desire at that moment to go to the Vukovar Hospital nor was this at all discussed. Page 8123 of the transcript refers to Mr. Cyrus's -- Cyrus Vance's desire to go to the Vukovar barracks and not the hospital. Eventually, at the end of the meeting, Colonel Mrksic said that the delegation should be taken to see whatever it wanted to see in Vukovar. The allegations of the Prosecution on page 76, paragraph 190, to the effect that on the 19th of November, 1991, Colonel Mrksic had been informed about the agreement reached in Zagreb between the JNA and the Croatian authorities does not -- do not stand. It is quite clear from ECMM documentation, that is Exhibit 315, that that mission received a report on the signed agreement on the 19th of November in the evening, namely, at 2241 hours by fax. So Colonel Mrksic could not have been acquainted with this, neither at that time nor during his talk with Vesna Bosanac, nor could have Vesna Bosanac have been acquainted with it as she herself says. There is no dispute, in fact, about the fact that the OTP has not proven that Colonel Mrksic received the text of this agreement in any way and at any time. As my learned colleague invoked this -- the statement of Vesna Bosanac in regard of this particular fact yesterday, I should like to read out for you what she says in the transcript. Page 672. "[In English] No. My understanding at that time was as follows: He said that the situation was now better because the shooting had ceased. He said we would now be better able to conduct an evacuation. Nevertheless, he himself didn't know exactly what it was that General Raseta had signed in Zagreb." [Interpretation] As regards the Zagreb Agreement, as a matter of fact, my learned colleague deliberately or fortuitously seems to fail to understand the substance of this agreement. Although the text of the agreement was not available in the field in Vukovar, not even on the 20th of November, because on that day Colonel Pavkovic says to the ICRC representative to show him a copy of that agreement. It does seem that the agreement itself states that it deals with the evacuation of the sick and wounded from the Vukovar Hospital of whom, according to the data, which were obviously obtained from the hospital on the date of the signature of the agreement. There were 40 severe patients and 360 or so wounded, a third of whom required stretchers. Those are the people encompassed by that agreement. So there were a total of around 400 of them. If the fact is borne in mind that there were no combat operations from the 18th of November and on and that no new patients were admitted, then that should be the final number of patients to be evacuated. When this number is compared with the number in Exhibit 321, the report of the ECMM, which states that at 1430 hours on the 20th of November, 82 bedridden wounded persons, and 263 mobile-wounded persons were evacuated and that there remained another 52 to be evacuated on the following day. The conclusion that can be drawn is that is precisely the number which the Zagreb Agreement refers to. And the number that was evacuated, in fact, in the presence of the ECMM and the ICRC, when this is borne in mind, it is not clear then what submissions my learned colleague is making in terms of violations of the Zagreb Agreement. Evidently the agreement was signed for the sake of the sick and wounded. They are persons to be supervised by the ICRC, but they are at the same time a category of persons which, under the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, could also be categorised as POWs and retained on the side of the capturing party. However, that obviously was not the case here. All the sick and wounded, at least that is what the numbers say, eventually reached Croatia. Thus it is not the category of people that the agreement refers to, as my learned colleague claims, but the agreement actually says the wounded and the sick. Then perhaps the question could be asked, And who are then the people who were taken out of the hospital in a convoy of six buses? Well, the answer would be that they are not a part of the Zagreb Agreement, which I again say never even reached the territory of Vukovar, and that they were either not at all expected there or, on the other hand, were brought there deliberately in order to create a problem with evacuation. Had that not been so, then Dr. Bosanac, when she was giving the numbers of the sick and wounded to Zagreb, probably on the 18th or on the 19th of November, would have certainly included in that number also those on whose healthy legs she would subsequently place plaster casts or whose healthy arms she would cut notches in or put bandages on their eyes and whose rifles she would then throw into the hospital garbage container. As the numbers of the wounded and sick reported by the hospital and those who were evacuated tally, then the people who were found at a hospital were, in fact, in a place in which they shouldn't have been. It was to be ascertained who they were and what they were and how come they found themselves in the hospital seeing that they were not sick. And some of them had to account for the fact why they were clothed in patient's or hospital clothes without being either sick nor being part of the hospital staff. It is precisely for such persons and their selections that a group of experts arrived from the security administration and the security department of the 1st MD. The more so as those who were removed from the hospital on the 20th were in fact those who did not transfer themselves to Velepromet on the previous day voluntarily, even though they were not under the auspices of the Vukovar Red Cross, even though they were not within the category of persons who were supposed to be in hospital. The removal of these persons actually does not amount to evacuation of the hospital, because that implies evacuation of those who are in hospital for treatment. The people who were separated that morning were combatants. And it seems to me that in Vukovar it was erroneous to divide people the way my learned colleague does and the indictment does to ex-combatants, political followers of the HDZ, journalists, the elderly, younger people, women, because from the testimonies of witnesses heard here, it follows that everybody had their place and role, their function, in the defence of Vukovar, within the units of the ZNG, the MUP, volunteer units, and the civilian part. That according to the statement of the witness Zvezdana Polovina, even journalists were active in rendering support to the defence staff of Vukovar. Can -- an HDZ activist be imagined who at that time was not a member of a military unit? I believe that that is in fact impossible. And finally my learned colleagues forget that it was the precisely the Prosecution witnesses who confirmed, here, to us all that there was a general mobilisation in Vukovar which encompassed according to the then law categories of persons from age 16 to the age of 65. Also the submission of my learned colleague yesterday in -- to the effect of ostensible differences in -- in the treatment of persons from Mitnica, as he will put it yesterday, soldiers, and persons from the hospital as he put it -- put it yesterday, terrorists and criminals, is completely faulty. If you recall his point in this particular regard, it was that in the first case lists were compiled, whereas in the second instance no lists were made, and that that in fact was a difference in the treatment of the two groups, a difference which was actually to determine their respective fates. Did my learned colleague lose sight of testimony of his own witnesses, namely both Mr. Vezmarovic and Mr. Vojinovic, and P-014. As far as I can see, and you will certainly recall this, in both cases were lists made in the hangar at Ovcara. In the first case it ended up with the security officer in Sremska Mitrovica, and in the second case, according to what the witness P-014 said, it ended up precisely on the table of yet another Prosecution witness and that is Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic. Witness P-014 in the transcript at page 7815 and page 7816 has the following to say -- Your Honours, perhaps it would be good now to go -- to move into private session. I'm not quite sure to what extent this statement I'm going to read will actually reveal the identity of the witness. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Okay, Mr. Vasic. Private, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was no difference whatsoever in the treatment of these groups as regards their registration and as regards their destination as well. The epilogue of the events would probably have been different had the security of the 80th Motorised Brigade not withdrawn late at night without any apparent reason. Therefore, according to the position of the Defence, this withdrawal is an incident and not a deliberate plan of the JCE as submitted by the Prosecutor. What does Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic tell us in regard to this list? On page 8974, lines 21 to 25: "[In English] No, I'm not saying that it didn't reach the command, but it didn't reach me or my desk. I assert that I didn't see it. Maybe somebody placed it on the desk and then took it again. These are all possibilities and guesses, and that's something that it's really not material here." [Interpretation] Now we shall leave this subject and pass to another one, and that is the allegation of the OTP on page 105 of their final brief. "[In English] The command of OG South received specific written orders from the 1st Military District warning them of the dangers of retaliation by the Vukovar TO and volunteers against the Vukovar population." [Interpretation] No piece of evidence presented in these proceedings demonstrates any such warning, nor does it follow from the testimony of any one witness. And the order which is Exhibit 409 and which is invoked by the Prosecution, it is not stated that this warning refers to the actions of TO Vukovar, nor does it indicate in any way whatsoever that this can be associated with the area of activity of this TO. And I should like also to remind you that this was -- this order was forwarded to all units that were subordinated to the command of the 1st Military District. In addition to this order, the command of OG South also received an order of the command of the 1st MD, which is Exhibit 415, this exhibit, which perhaps, has been the most exploited one by the Prosecution in this case. According to this -- under this order, according to the claim of the Prosecution, Mrksic, with his written order, warned his subordinates of practices to which the command of the 1st Military District had also been pointing to. This is also attested to by OTP witnesses. For instance, Witness Trifunovic, and Defence witnesses for Mr. Mrksic, Colonel Lesanovic, Colonel Gluscevic, Lieutenant Colonel Danilovic, as well as Defence witnesses for the Defence of Mr. Sljivacanin, Lieutenant Colonel Panic, and Major Vukasinovic. Colonel Mrksic pointed to the danger which was actually the substance of these orders; also, in his order of the 20th of November, 1991, which constitutes Exhibit 419. Namely, he warned the commanders of towns that they should secure and control the security of property and persons in their respective zones of responsibility. Also when he comments on the visit of Mr. Seselj to Vukovar, my learned colleague does something that we have been pointing out to the Bench at all times, namely, on page 110 of his final brief, my learned friend states that the command of OG South had to allow this visit invoking the testimony of Witness Trifunovic, although, on page 8287 of the transcript, Witness Trifunovic has the following to say: "[In English] In practice, what would happen with his visits is something that I really don't know. Who authorised him or issued permission for him to do that, I don't know that. But as far as the procedure is concerned, I'm sure some people could explain how that went. All I heard was that he came and that he was at Petrova Gora, that he was in the south detachment 1, that he was raising morale working on the motivation, and I think that Colonel Mrksic didn't issue permission for that either. Perhaps when he found out he was just reconciled to the fact." [Interpretation] It is quite clear from this that, precisely the witness invoked by the Prosecution, states that Colonel Mrksic did not issue any permission to Mr. Seselj to come to Vukovar. Furthermore, on page 111, the OTP suggests that the conflict in Vukovar also went on after November the 18th, and that Witness Trifunovic spoke about the problems that were created by members of the TO but also by volunteers and by paramilitary units, and of which Colonel Mrksic had allegedly been informed, and in the conclusion of the OTP, failed to take any measures in order to -- failed to take any measures. The Witness Trifunovic on page 8150 states the following: "[In English] I heard that there were problems on all three days, on the 18th in Mitnica, but these were minor problems which are quite realistically possible in such a situation. I heard about 19, too, that there were problems with the transfer of people from the captured parts of town, primarily from the central part of town, to Velepromet, the barracks in Ovcara, that there were problems with the local population as well as members of the TO defence who are from that area." [Interpretation] And then, as regards his assessment of the situation, what his assessment of the situation in the command of OG South was, he says on page 8281: "Q. Yesterday you stated that all the information that came down to verbal abuse or light physical contact as you put it? "A. Yes." [Interpretation] Therefore, not even the witness himself, the one relied on by the Prosecution, didn't say that there existed information indicating that the events were such that they could lead to any serious incidents. Also, he didn't claim that volunteers and paramilitaries participated in these events but, rather, just members of the local TO. On page 138, paragraph 382, my learned friend brings the views of Colonel Bogdan Vujic about having informed Colonel Mrksic and Major Sljivancanin about events at Velepromet on the 19th of November. And that on the following day, 17 corpses were found in Velepromet and that they were buried at the military cemetery with the logistical support of officers of Colonel Mrksic. As for the personality and character traits of witness Bogdan Vujic, we spoke about that in our final brief concerning the validity of the conclusion of my learned friend that he was an honest and decent man. This is something that Mr. Domazet will address a bit later. It remains for me to say here that his story, the one he invented, fortunately, had its own eyewitness, and that is the eyewitness who is invoked by Bogdan Vujic himself. This is precisely Branko Korica, the witness who was heard here, and based on his testimony, we can see exactly which part of the story of Bogdan Vujic was correct and which part wasn't. In this specific case, it is not true that he either informed Colonel Mrksic or Major Sljivacanin, whom he didn't even see that night, as well as that no bodies were found, bodies that were allegedly buried with the assistance of Colonel Mrksic. Had my learned friend wanted to present firsthand evidence to the Trial Chamber, he would have called Mr. Kijanovic to come in and testify. Witness Vujic says about Kijanovic that he allegedly told him about burying those corpses himself. You will admit that that would have been logical had he done that. However, preparing for this case, my learned friend knew that Witness Kijanovic, in his testimony before the court in Belgrade, did not confirm these allegations by Witness Vujic. Therefore, he didn't call him to testify, and it all boiled down to the hearsay evidence. Naturally, Colonel Mrksic neither saw Vujic in the might between the 20th and 21st of November, nor were the corpses buried by Lesanovic at the time with the assistance -- I apologise, not Lesanovic but Kijanovic. Buried by Kijanovic with the assistance of the logistical unit of Mr. Mrksic. These are just pure fabrications of Witness Vujic that my learned friend has accepted. On the same page, in paragraph 383, my learned friend claims that Colonel Mrksic involved -- or engaged the units of TO Vukovar in the triage and transport of prisoners. That doesn't stand from any piece of evidence or testimony heard before this Trial Chamber. Colonel Mrksic had nothing to do either with the selection or transport of prisoners. And this entire task was performed by security organs due to the nature of the task itself. They had come to Vukovar in November -- on the 19th of November, 1991, precisely in order to perform this task. Colonel Mrksic never issued any kind of order for the TO Vukovar units to participate in any similar operation. Thus, this is a pure insinuation that is not supported by any material, formal, or written piece of evidence. Also in paragraph 385, my learned friend brings forward some arbitrary conclusions concerning Colonel Mrksic. He claims that on the 19th of November, Colonel Mrksic gave assignments to his subordinates about a joint plan -- or, rather, concerning joint criminal enterprise, which was the evacuation of the so-called criminals, as he termed them, from the hospital. If you look at Exhibit 419, it will be clear that this is not true and that by way of this order, precisely, the evacuation of the sick, wounded, and civilian hospital staff was ordered and not the evacuation of the so-called criminals, as termed by my learned friend, whose transport and triage was dealt by the competent organs. Your Honours, I would now like to ask you to turn into private session, because this witness testified in a closed session, and this is a very sensitive witness whose name was mentioned yesterday by my learned friend, and this is a very important witness, and I will have to read out a large portion of his testimony. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There is not a single piece of evidence that can support the argument of my learned friend that Colonel Mrksic ordered Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, whose unit in its area of responsibility guarded prisoners of war, to withdraw the military police company and turn over prisoners to the TO Vukovar members for further guarding. This argument was not uttered by Vojnovic himself either, nor was it uttered by witness Vukosavljevic, his security organ chief, or Witness Vezmarovic, company commander of the military police company or Witness Karanfilov who allegedly conveyed the order. Not even chief of staff, Lieutenant Colonel Panic said that. Even the omniscient witness Trifunovic has no knowledge of this. These arguments of the Prosecution are not supported by logic either, the arguments put forward on page 102 of the final brief. If we were to rely on the tried and trusted claims of the Prosecution such as who could have done it if it weren't for the commander, then the Prosecutor would first have to explain several points. First, how come Mrksic issued an order when he was not in Negoslavci, or at least, if they claim that he was in Negoslavci, why did he do that through the security organ with whom he had no direct contact? Why didn't he do it directly through the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade which whom he had regular contact and whom he saw that same evening? I will remind you that in his testimony here, Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic said that he did not receive any order from Colonel Mrksic about withdrawing security detail but, rather, that he took the comment he heard as the reason for withdrawing. That comment didn't even suggest anything that we as laymen could use in order to conclude something like that. It was definitely not sufficient for a professional soldier such as Vojnovic, especially if I were to remind you that Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic in his career was a battalion commander of the military police and dealt with security affairs. It is the position of the Defence that this sentence which Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, who in our view is the main culprit for the tragedy that took place at Ovcara, was understood by him, providing that it was uttered in the first place. The only possible interpretation in our view would be this: What are you doing there? Why weren't you using 1.000 soldiers and tanks which I had resubordinated to you in order to ensure law and order in the Grabovo, Ovcara, and Jakupovac sector? This is why Colonel Mrksic could not have ordered to him, who was commander of this sector, to withdraw the security detail. We heard here both the theory and provisions of the rules of service based on which it is clear that during the night Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic should not have withdrawn. He should not have allowed for the security detail to withdraw from the Ovcara farm, the security which was deployed there on the basis of his own order at 1600 hours. Even had something of that nature been ordered by anyone else, Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic as an experienced officer knew that he had to request an explicit written order for withdrawal rather than assume, as he put it here, what somebody else thought. Even if he had received a written order, which was not the case in this instance, he still who should not have withdrawn the military police during the night if he believed the situation to be critical. What he had to do under the circumstances was refuse to carry out such an order and to address himself to the commander of the 1st Military District and intervene for the execution of such an order to stop. Therefore, we were unable to find a single piece of evidence indicating that Colonel Mrksic ordered anything of the sort except for what is offered by my learned friend, which are the statement of Lieutenant Colonel Panic as to who could have done it if it weren't Colonel Mrksic, as well as the statement of Mr. Sljivacanin Defence expert Mr. Vuga who again said, Who else could have done it but Colonel Mrksic. Nobody either saw the order or heard the order, nor did the person receiving the order ever claim that it was issued by Colonel Mrksic. Given the state of affairs in this instance, any similar conclusion is baseless. Now I will go back to Lieutenant Colonel Panic and his claim about the alleged instructions concerning the surrender of prisoners that he received for the government cabinet session. When he was asked to surrender them to the cabinet based on this -- these instructions, when he was asked who was supposed to carry out this surrender based on the instructions, the answer was, "I don't know." "Was that you?" Answer, "No". "Where was surrender supposed to take place?" The answer, "I don't know." "Where was this surrender to take place?" The answer, "I don't know." "Who was supposed to write up the lists for surrender?" Answer, "I don't know." So what kind of a command representative is he as he described himself? He went there to convey the order for the surrender of certain people, and he said himself that he was authorised to do that but didn't know who was supposed to surrender them, when, or where, or why. How come this is not mentioned by a single word in his notebook? I think that due to these reasons his testimony should not be accepted. It should also not be accepted due to the portion which is contradictory to the testimony of Bogdan Vujic about the session itself and what Lieutenant Colonel Panic said about what had transpired during that session, but I will speak more of this later. I wanted to highlight something else here. It is clear to me why witnesses Trifunovic and Panic do not speak truth about the events of the 20th of November, especially when it comes to the role of Mr. Mrksic and his trip to Belgrade. Deputy Commander Lieutenant Colonel Panic and Chief Operations Officer, Trifunovic, upon the departure of the commander on the 20th of November in the evening, were the ones in command of the unit. They drafted -- or, rather, one of them drafted and the other one signed the famous Exhibit 422 about resubordination, which is based on the alleged order of the command of the 1st Military District, number 115-151, dated the 20th of November, which in reality is not an order. It deals with the issue of resubordination, and as I said, it is not an order but, rather, just a plain report. In this order, which has a false base, I'm referring to Exhibit 422, a false foundation, they used terms which cannot be found in any other order from that period of time. They're using terms such as "Seselj's men," or "Seseljevci," or "Sumadinac" or men from Sumadija. If we look at Exhibit 444 dated the 22nd of November, 1991, dealing with the cooperation of the Vukovar TO with the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade, this is to say about the cooperation, then it becomes clear that there was no resubordination there whatsoever. Thus, the content of Exhibit 422 is false as well. It would have been natural, following the 18th of November and completion of main combat operations in the liberation of the town, for all TO units to return, TO units which were within temporary units such as assault detachments. It would have been natural for them to return to the command of their staff. Your Honours, is this a good time for a break? JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Yes, Mr. Vasic. We will have a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Mr. Vasic, may we ask you to be very aware of the time. We will give you five minutes more that we have given to Mr. Moore, but please be aware of the time because otherwise the schedule will be impossible to maintain. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Speaking of the group of officers that the OTP call as their witnesses, we have already pointed out that, in the case of many of them, it would have been far more logical to find them included in the indictment instead, especially those officers of the 80th Motorised Brigade who, within their area of responsibility, guarded the prisoners of war who were eventually struck by the crime that occurred. The commander of the 80th Brigade, Vojnovic, used none of the units resubordinated to him by Colonel Mrksic in order to secure the territory of Grabovo, Ovcara, and Jakupovac, which means he didn't need them and which means he had sufficient manpower to secure the hangar and the prisoners. He is the principal culprit for not preventing the withdrawal of his unit from the hangar, which is something that I have already addressed. He allowed Witness P-014, whose duty was to control the facility and whatever went on inside it, to refuse to perform his function, and even to refuse to return to the command post of his own unit unless the assistance of military police were secured for him to guard his own command post. He did get the security required from Colonel Vojnovic and eventually returned to the command post, ordering to fire at anyone attempting to enter the command building during that night. And people were being taken away at a distance of a mere 200 or 300 metres from this very place throughout the night. As to all of these events and also what happened the following morning, Vojnovic did not tell what he knew anyone from the superior command, which is something that he himself has claimed. Instead, the next day, he sent a delegation from Kragujevac to Ovcara to visit the command and the witness that I have just mentioned. None of these witnesses were included in the OTP indictment, nor was, for that matter, Bogdan Vujic, if indeed what we heard from him during his testimony is true. He claimed to have been the commander of the triage of the persons at Velepromet on the 19th of November. He claimed that he was given the assignment by the security administration and he performed this task on behalf of the Supreme Command. He claims that during the evacuation some persons were taken away and killed, and yet he did nothing to stop this or indeed to arrest or even, if necessary, kill the perpetrators which he names as Topola and Crevar. As a security officer on this mission, he was certainly authorised to take steps of that nature. As a high-ranking officer of the security administration, he didn't do this, yet he tried to shift the blame for his own omissions to Colonel Mrksic and Major Sljivacanin during his testimony before this Trial Chamber. Fortunately, his story is almost entirely illogical and as such has been refuted in its entirety by the testimony of Witness Branko Korica. As to the group of witnesses called by the Prosecution and some of the witnesses called by Mr. Sljivacanin's Defence team, that had previously been dropped by the OTP, these witnesses are officers who faced a potential indictment or at least faced the status of suspects. Based on their evidence, we were able to tell that they tailored their evidence with a view to escaping criminal responsibility, their own or that of their own -- or that of their close associates. The objective was to protect themselves and their associates to the degree possible. This becomes clear if you study the evidence they gave in criminal proceedings throughout the 1990s and compare these to the evidence provided by these persons over the last couple of years, specifically before this court. Some of these witnesses told us that meetings had been held as well as debates between the witnesses themselves, witnesses of this nature. Trials were monitored and transcripts were studied in order to ascertain who said what at a certain trial, what sort of things were being said and made public. The only person left with no protection at all, left exposed and left to dry, as it were, as a convenient scapegoat was Commander Colonel Mile Mrksic. There was finger pointing at him by those whose task was to conduct the triage. Organs of the security administration of the 1st Army. Vukasinovic who was in charge of the transportation section or for that matter by those people whose duty was to guard the prisoners at Ovcara such as the officers of the 18th Brigade the ones I've already mentioned, and finally those who after the departure of the commander on the 28th of November were the command of OG South between the evening of the 20th and the afternoon of the 22nd these persons being the chief of staff and the chief operative officer of the Guards Brigade. There is one thing that no one has raised during this trial. The issue wasn't even raised by the OTP in their final brief, for that matter. If things were the way they suggest they were, that is if Mrksic had ordered the withdrawal, why then does Witness Borce Karanfilov not say in plain terms before this Chamber that he had simply been ordered to do this by his commander, to go to Ovcara and to withdraw the security detail of the 80th Brigade? If that is true, the witness escapes personal responsibility or indeed the responsibility of Mr. Sljivacanin on who's behalf he testified. The only reason he ended up not saying this was precisely this: Colonel Mrksic never ordered anyone to withdraw the security detail from the Ovcara farm. As to who did this while waiting for him to leave for Belgrade, now that is something that we have not been able to ascertain throughout this trial. Another thing that will remain a mystery is who issued the order or why. Documents have gone missing, that is one thing. And the other is my learned friend simply chose not to call certain witnesses. One thing is certain. The person who issued this order was not Colonel Mrksic. Had he done this, then between the government session and the withdrawal of the security there would not have elapsed over seven hours. It would have been well known who was doing the hand-over, who was involved in the hand-over, and where. The order to withdraw would not have gone through security clerks but, rather, through the commanders of the unit within whose area of responsibility these persons were and indeed under whose command they were. Likewise, it is certain that this would have been a subject raised at the meeting with the regular briefing which in fact was not the case, not even when the events at Ovcara were discussed. Finally, this would no doubt have been entered into the war log, which was not the case either. As for the government session itself, even the OTP tendered under Rule 98 bis statements made by government ministers who took part in that session claiming that no decision was reached in that respect on that day in Vukovar. Perhaps the most relevant witness on this is Witness Jaksic, whom Mrksic explicitly instructed on the 28th of November to convey to the president of the Supreme Court his refusal to surrender these persons. Just as interesting is the testimony of Colonel Sisic, a Sljivacanin Defence witness, who claims that on the 20th of November while the buses were still in the barracks, he called Mrksic. He claims that Mrksic told him to guard them at all cost until the government reached a decision on their eventual fate. However, there is no inherent logic to this evidence. This officer had no need to call Mrksic directly since protection measures had already been taken by Witness Vukasinovic as he already told us he was in charge of the convoy by the barracks and town commander who was present, Major Branislav Lukic, and by the Guards Brigade chief of staff who was also there, Miodrag Panic. The commander's eyes and ears, which is how my learned friend Mr. Moore prefers to refer to him. Had that been the decision taken, then the convoy would have stayed right there waiting for that decision. They would not have just moved on. Yet it was before the session itself that he went to Ovcara. It's OTP witnesses that we have on the record as saying that. They were the people on the buses. If that decision had been taken, it would have been recorded on a slip of paper in that notepad used by Lieutenant Colonel Panic, which apparently, as he said, he carried around instead of an official notebook whenever he went to official meetings. We would be able to find decisions there, not just a handful of sentences jotted down and no reference at all to any decision whatsoever. This same Panic, controlling any entries into the war log, would have asked for this to be recorded unless this had already been done, and it hadn't. Probably this would have been the subject of a report submitted to the 1st Military District, even perhaps the report that Lieutenant Colonel Panic wrote himself on the 21st of November, 1991. There is no way this sort of information could have been suppressed. Zivota Panic would have known through his own organs, through his own commissions monitoring the Vukovar evacuation. Generals Mile Babic -- General Mile Babic and Colonel Petkovic would have known who sent out their own security troops from Sid to conduct a triage. Eventually, General Aca Vasiljevic would have known the chief of the security administration who on that same mission sent out one of his own teams and was present in the area at the critical point in time. Finally, we heard evidence from Mr. Karan, that even Goran Hadzic, the Prime Minister at the time, was an associate of the military security service. The SSNO should have known. They should have known about his contacts to the officers, to Colonel Pavkovic and Colonel Terzic. The SSNO was involved in the negotiations on how the evacuation to the Vukovar Hospital was to be conducted through Colonel Pavkovic, General Raseta, Admiral Brovet, and Colonel Memisevic, persons involved in these events, even in some case as decision-makers. Bearing all of this in mind, was it possible to conclude that Colonel Mrksic had taken the decision to surrender these persons to the government as Miodrag Panic would have it and yet for this to remain a secret and go entirely unrecorded? Is it possible to hold him responsible for that? This was outside his authority, and this is clearly confirmed by such exhibits as the order by General Vlado Stojanovic, dated the 19th of November. The hand-over of prisoners took place without his approval. And we also have Aleksandar Vasiljevic's telegram, the telegram he sent to Major Sljivacanin to show the same thing. This sort of decision could not have been concealed, bearing in mind all the circumstances. I don't believe it could have been concealed from the representatives of the ICRC or the international monitors, for that matter, who, on the same day they entered the hospital, found out that people had been taken away even as the buses were still waiting in the barracks. Therefore, the answer is no, there is no way that Colonel Mrksic could have taken such a decision. There is no way that he would have ever have been able or in a position to take such a decision. Had he taken this decision, then Miodrag Panic would not have been right there at Ovcara watching the prisoners leave. Security officers Kijanovic, Tomic, and Mucan [phoen], as well as the rest of them, would not have been there inside the hangar or around the hangar in the afternoon and evening hours on that day. Finally, the prisoners would not have remained under guard until 10.30 that night when the security people eventually withdrew. Had Mrksic decided for those persons to be surrendered, Captain Vukosavljevic, the leaders of the counter-intelligence group from Sid would not have told Captain Vukosavljevic not to investigate Ovcara but, rather, to try and look after the safety of his own unit. Finally, had Mrksic decided that, the exact entry relating to his departure for Belgrade would not have been inaccurate. What we have heard is he never took that flight with Major Tesic on the morning of the 21st of November. Had Mrksic been there, this sort of order could never have been taken, nor would it have ever been possible to withdraw the security detail from the Ovcara farm. These are examples of how the Prosecution decided not to indict those who really are to blame for the crime at Ovcara in order to elicit their testimony against the already-accused Mrksic. This creates a bias in relation to their evidence, and we have seen this at work. I do hope that the Honourable Chamber will eventually confirm this and rule on it. Drawing conclusions as to why the final brief of my learned friend says what it says and taking into account what in the submission of our defence would be a valid assessment of the evidence, we have reached the conclusion that the reason must be that the OTP did not pay sufficient attention to evidence given by witnesses in cross-examination or in re-examination. In order to obtain, therefore, a complete mosaic of the events and a valid assessment of the existence of the liability of the accused, it is necessary to simultaneously read the brief of my learned colleague with the final briefs of the Defence, because only then will it be -- will it be possible for each individual question to be elucidated from all the necessary sides. I shall say a few words about the experts which the OTP called here. First of all, about Mr. Theunens, who is in fact a member of the Prosecution team and who according to his own testimony participated in the shaping of the indictment in the compilation of the questions to be put to the witnesses and the only thing which he did not do was to question the witnesses in the courtroom, but he did question them outside the courtroom, and we have testimony to that effect. He is on the OTP's payroll, and he is temporarily employed there, and we deem that his account cannot be objective and acceptable, while the material evidence attached to his findings can be accepted and appraised. As regards the other expert witness, General Pringle, with his responses and with his attempt at sustaining the unsustainable where Witness Vojnovic is concerned, he has compromised his expertise and his objectivity. I'm just going to mention the references, Your Honours, because I do not have the time to read it all. These are transcripts number 11064 to 11096, and then 11070 to 11071, and 11093 to 11095. In brief, this witness did not have an insight into a single -- he did not inspect a single doctrine or document of general People's Defence, total People's Defence and social protection that he pretended to give expert opinions about [no interpretation]. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Sorry, interpreters have a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He did not have access to the documents. He did not have access to the documents of the 80th Motorised Brigade nor those of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nor did he know that the command of the 1st Military District had set up a team that monitored, that followed the evacuation in Vukovar. And the greatest mistake was perhaps that he thought that the Zagreb Agreement had regulated the evacuation of prisoners of war, which is actually inadmissible lack of knowledge of the content of this document, so that his expertise, in our view, cannot be taken into account as grounded in the judicial decision that will be reached. I shall now speak very briefly about what my learned colleague referred to yesterday when we talk about the rules on the application of the rules of International Law of War. I should just like to say that my colleague forgot to attach Articles 1 to 4 of the rule in question. Article 1 states that it is applicable only in the event of an international conflict, so that the different modality has to be found in respect of the content of these provisions that my learned colleague invokes in this context. And the second omission which he made is his claim that the war log was -- was actually kept from the 1st of October to the 23rd of November. Now, it was actually kept until the 22nd of November, when the OG South actually handed over the zone of responsibility to the 80th Motorised Brigade. This -- this is -- this is something that you will see from Exhibit 401, which is the war log. And finally, and I believe that this is the last question and it stems from your question yesterday, Your Honour, Judge Thelin, and it is connected to General Aleksandar Vasiljevic and his presence in Vukovar, it is the position of the Defence that there exists serious claims that he was in Negoslavci also in the night between the 20th of November and the 21st of November, and that could also be concluded on the basis of the testimony of Witness Karanfilov who states that on the same day when he brought the Commissioner for Vukovar to Negoslavci and saw the buses in the barracks and a group of locals around the buses that on that same day in the evening General Vasiljevic came to the house where the security organs were accompanied by General Tumanov. This is not an a customary thing for two security generals to come on such a visit. There had to be a very special reason indeed for that. If the statement of Karanfilov is to be lent credence that that could have happened only on the 20th of November, because it was only on that date that there were buses in the barracks surrounded by people, and it was only on that day that he could have taken the Commissioner from the barracks to Negoslavci. Why can this be of consequence? Well, if the head of the administration was the one who was deciding on the fate of the POWs and who was in charge of the exchange for the Labredo [phoen] group, then he could have decided the fate of the captives from Ovcara as well. But whether he had indeed done so is something that we could not actually verify because my learned colleague from the Prosecution actually chose not to call General Vasiljevic as a witness although he had been on the 65 ter list. After this assessment of the final brief and the closing arguments of my learned colleague, I am drawing to a close and I will give the floor to my learned colleague, Vladimir Domazet who will actually conclude the closing arguments for the Defence. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. The problem is we have only five minutes to go for Mr. Domazet, so he will have to be very short. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems that I only have the time to say good afternoon. Unfortunately, I had envisaged about 40 minutes for my statement, so in the five minutes allocated to me, I will have to pick and choose from it and say a few words that in view of the fact that Mr. Vasic has left me some time to contribute to the Defence statement myself, but I will have to abridge that as well. As regards Vujic, I would like to say a few words about some very important things that our learned colleague, Moore, also insisted on yesterday and that has to do with coming from Velepromet on that night. At that time he certainly could not have seen Colonel Mrksic, not only owing to the fact that it was far after midnight when the commander was already in bed and only the officer on duty could have been in the operations group room, but also because of the fact that the witness's -- the testimony of Witness Korica is eminently clear to the effect that he had come from Velepromet before Vujic had, because in contrast to him who walked, he had come by car and that throughout that period while he was there, that is, he didn't see Colonel Mrksic, so that Vujic could not have seen him either, Vujic who came much later, and then he went together with Korica, that is to say they all went to bed. And just another thing. It is really totally illogical and quite unacceptable that an officer of the kind of Mrksic would have listened to those -- would have heard the words uttered here by Vujic without responding to that in any way whatsoever. That is unacceptable. It is unbelievable. It is improbable, because Vujic could not have really fabricated a response to the briefing, to the reporting that never was, in fact. Regrettably I cannot dwell on this in any longer. I shall just focus for a couple of minutes on the role of Colonel Mrksic himself to say that at times it emanated here from statements that his role was solely to look after or see about what would be happening with this group of 200 or so prisoners. One should bear in mind that especially during those final days the commander of the operations group had to look after several thousand soldiers under his command, several thousand civilians who demanded to leave the city after the combat had died down, with the situation being as it was still very insecure. The town was mined. He had many problems to address and solve. And having said this, I should like to add that not a single piece of evidence was presented here to the effect that during the morning when the triage took place in the hospital, had commander Mrksic at any moment been informed whether it had been carried out, how many people had been included in the triage process, who the people were, and it is claimed that allegedly he handed over those people to some government at a meeting that has already been referred to here repeatedly, and I'm not going to repeat that myself. Just a few words in conclusion about Mrksic himself, who was actually born in Croatia where he pursued his schooling and where he lived. He finished high school in precisely Vukovar, and he pursued his education, his military education, reaching -- attaining the highest ranks for the most part of the time in this elite unit, the kind of that the Guards Brigade was. He would never have attained such positions, and held such ranks had anything been there to indicate in any way whatsoever that this was the sort of person who could do anything bad to people of another ethnicity, who could do anything wrong by them. I should like to remind you that as an officer and as a human being he was referred to by all the witnesses who were asked the question and who took the stand here. He was referred in the nicest terms -- referred to in the nicest terms by all such witnesses as a person and as a commander. And finally, in contrast to many who held much lower ranks and held much lower positions in these wars but managed to amass fortunes, General Mrksic was retired and lived with his wife and three children, three daughters whom he's still supporting, namely who are still living off his pension, and in fact until he surrendered to this Tribunal he did manual work at a market in Belgrade in order to make ends meet, which actually shows best what kind of a person he is. Unfortunately, I really have no time, and I can only reiterate our submission, our proposal and our submission which is the Defence considers that the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused Mrksic has committed the acts that he is charged with, and that the Defence proposes to this honourable Tribunal to acquit the accused of all charges. Thank you. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. We will turn now to the Defence of Mr. Radic. Mr. Borovic has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, distinguished colleagues from the Prosecution, I shall start with a quotation by our great poet of Petar Petrovic Njegos who said, "Fear of life often taints honour." And this is a principle that Miroslav Radic often followed in his life and that is why he decided to come forward and tell the truth before this august Tribunal so that the Croatian public and the public in Serbia and elsewhere would know what his role had been in this entire thing. And we should like to say that the accused Radic and the defence of Radic condemn the heinous act and crime at Ovcara as an appalling act and that we all share this feeling. The indictment charges the accused with the violation of laws and customs of war and crimes against humanity. In our final brief, we have dealt with everything which is dealt with under Article 3 of the Statute. The Prosecution's final brief submissions in detail as regards Article 3 of the Statute and as regards Article 5 of the Statute, we can only add that the Defence feels, at the very outset, that the Prosecution has failed to prove the allegations of the Prosecution beyond reasonable doubt, that is to say, that the accused had been aware of the widespread or systematic attack or of its context of a widespread or systematic attack or that his actions were part of that attack. In addition to that, the Prosecution, both in its case and in its final brief, failed to prove that the accused was aware of the fact that the Serbian forces had taken all settlements in Eastern Slavonia, as the Prosecution claims. The Prosecution also failed to prove that Miroslav Radic was informed or could have been informed or put on notice or was aware that an attack of that nature was in progress. He, as a company commander, came to Vukovar, was given a task which was limited to just one street, and he carried out this task pursuant to the orders of his commander. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal has established that one has to prove that the accused not only had an intention to commit a crime that he's charged with, but also had to know that there was an attack on civilian population. We heard the account of Miroslav Radic during his testimony. Another thing that one also needs to point out is that he had to risk at least to have his acts become part of that attack. I don't think that any of these three elements which constitute the elements of violation of Article 5 were proven by the Prosecution. In paragraph 139, the Prosecution speaks about the initial selection at the hospital on the 18th and 19th of November. Yesterday, we heard an inspired submission by my learned friend, Mr. Lunny, who said, with respect to this, what Dr. Njavro stated during his testimony. What is especially curious is what was inferred concerning this witness. They said that if the Chamber does not prove Dr. Njavro, then definitely somebody from the Guards Motorised Brigade participated in this initial selection. The Prosecution also believes that if Dr. Njavro was wrong and wrongly conveyed the fact concerning Dr. Dejanovic, then it doesn't mean that everything else said by Dr. Njavro wasn't true either. The Defence believes this is something that should not be ignored. Every witness who took an oath before this court, who took a solemn declaration, not only Witness P-024 concerning whom we requested that an investigation be instituted against him, has to speak the truth in front of every court, and this applies to this witness as well, regardless of the fact that he was a minister of health of Croatia. His testimony was discredited by the testimony of officer Karan, an honest officer, who learned that Dr. Radomir Dejanovic was mentioned in this context and he explained very explicitly to this Trial Chamber that he was the one who asked Dr. Njavro whether he knew Dr. Dejanovic, and he said that he was the one who did all the acts that the Prosecution wrongly attributes to the accused Radic. He was captain of security organ, and without knowing what Karan was going to testify, the Defence kept pointing out that Radic was not a security captain, was not a member who belonged to counter-intelligence service, which is something that Dr. Njavro claimed. He said that he not only inquired about his friend Dr. Radomir Dejanovic but also in front of this court he explained who the members of Dr. Dejanovic's assembly were, how old he was, where he had studied and so on. We put to Witness Njavro that Dejanovic could not have gone to school with Radic and that he had completed his college in Belgrade, that he was 10 years older than Radic, and that on the other hand Radic had graduated from the military academy in Sarajevo and that he was 10 years younger. However, the intention to trick the Chamber to assist the Prosecution or perhaps some other reason which we are unaware of, motivated this witness to stand by his original claims. However, owing to the conditions which this Trial Chamber created for the Defence counsel and for the fair trial of their accused, we conducted an investigation, and I will put this in very mild terms and say that Njavro was wrong when he said that Captain Radic arrested him and took to Sremska Mitrovica. Witness Karan said, I was the one who did that. I was the security organ and I did that task in accordance with the law and this is something that many other witnesses confirm. Then Dr. Njavro proceeds to say something about the events with Ante Maric. He placed it in the context of acts allegedly performed by Radic, and Witness Antic said, "I was the one who spoke to him. I said, take off the yellow boots, because otherwise you could have problems." All of this are the elements which Dr. Njavro tried to place before the Trial Chamber, but these facts were not true. So not only is it not true that somebody from the Guards Motorised Brigade participated in this election process and abused -- abused patients in the hospital, but simply the Trial Chamber cannot rely on this witness because he did not say the truth. Now, Witness P-012, who on page of the transcript 3727/5, when it comes to the date, when a witness said that he toured the hospital with Kuzmic, Njavro said that it was Radic, whereas this witness says that I know that this was a captain with a moustache. I could recognise him if I saw him, and I saw this captain in the movie "100 Days of Vukovar." Your Honours, we introduced that piece of evidence here which is Exhibit 171. I hope that any dilemmas concerning this have been resolved by the Defence, and perhaps this could be of assistance to the Prosecution. Perhaps this could point them in some other direction when it comes to this witness. The Prosecution interviewed Dr. Radomir Dejanovic, and he said, in order to round off the conclusion, he said, "I do not know Captain Miroslav Radic." In paragraph 144, on the other -- of the Prosecution, there is a position put forward that Radic took part in the process of identification and selection of the alleged criminals acting pursuant to the orders of Sljivacanin. In order to support their allegations, the Prosecution brought Witness P-030 to testify here. This witness, P-030, claims that he heard, and this is the only sentence which several years ago placed Captain Miroslav Radic in the context of joint criminal enterprise. The Defence has succeeded, and I will explain this further, in establishing that this witness didn't say the truth either. Perhaps it is not a popular method to say of the Prosecution witnesses that they did not speak the truth, but I apologise, Your Honours. Except for Witness Njavro, all other Prosecution witnesses who allegedly agitate -- aggravate the position of Accused Radic were protected witnesses who hid themselves from the public. This is why the public will never learn -- both the public in Croatia and the public in Serbia will never learn about their testimonies. Even once the judgement is handed down, the public will not know what evidence was adduced because all of the evidence was adduced in private or closed sessions. So this Witness P-030 claims that he heard, when Sljivacanin said, "Captain Radic, search the people." We asked him and this witness gave several statements concerning this fact and he said the following: "This is a captain who had four stars on his shoulders. He was 35 to 40 old. He was 175 centimetres to 180 centimetres tall." It was put to him that Captain Miroslav Radic at the time was 29. It also put to him that he was 192 centimetres tall. My learned friend yesterday claimed that this was the height of Sljivacanin. It was put to this witness that he was a captain who had three stars, but normally he didn't have rank insignia on his uniform, and a lot of witnesses testified to this. We also showed a photograph showing him without insignia on his shoulders. This was something that was not done during wartime. Rather, a badge was worn with insignia. He did not have a beret on his head, no kind of burgundy beret nor did he wear an olive drab uniform on the 20th of November, 1991. We clearly stated, that on the 20th of November, Miroslav Radic wore a camouflage uniform. We heard how Witness 2D4 confirmed this and he also confirmed that he didn't wear his rank insignia on his shoulders. The witness -- the Defence impeached and discredited this witness not only when it comes to him seeing Radic on the 20th of November conducting the selection and identification, but he was also discredited by the witnesses of Mr. Sljivacanin. Sljivacanin himself, in his testimony before the Court, said that Miroslav Radic on the 20th of November, 1991 at the time when the evacuation was conducted was not present at the hospital. Witness Simic, commander of the military police company, which secured the evacuation, conducted the search of the prisoners, escorted them to the buses and so on, said firmly before this Court under oath that Captain Miroslav Radic was not present nor did he participate in triage, search, or selection of the prisoners. Paunovic, a witness who explained in detail his role at the hospital here, when asked directly, said that Miroslav Radic could not have had any role nor did he have any role considering that his military police company was present or, rather, his subordinate company commander Simic and himself. We asked Simic directly whether Radic participated in this selection process. He said on page -- or, rather, Paunovic said on page 14182/24. And then we asked Simic, since I as Defence counsel failed to put this question directly to Paunovic, I asked him how old he was in 1991, and he said that he was born in 1956, which means that at the relevant period of time he was 35. He was 175 to 180 centimetres tall, which means at least that this witness could have seen Witness Paunovic but definitely not Captain Radic. When the search was conducted and triage and when the people about were escorted to the buses witnesses such as Dragutin Berghofer were present as were Witnesses P-031, Emil Cakalic, Witness P-009, and Witness P-012. His Honour Judge Parker enabled the Defence at the time to put to the Witness P-030 other things that witnesses had stated according to the rules which in force at the time. None of them heard anybody mention or call out the name of Captain Radic. All of them stood together in that group in front of the hospital some one to two metres away from Witness P-030. My learned friend, Mr. Moore at one point in time, tried to explain this before the Trial Chamber. A question was put to Berghofer, and he said that it seemed that that man had no rank insignia. He was about 40 years old. Whereas Witness P-031 said it was a lieutenant, a lieutenant who conducted the search, and that same person was present in the barracks and took out those 15 people off a bus. The Prosecutor insisted for quite a while on this issue. You can see this on transcript page 3240 to 3248, and in the end it was clear that that was the same person that was a lieutenant. Naturally, nobody ever mentioned Captain Miroslav Radic. This Trial Chamber knows that the problem of identification is a very significant one.
