The Prosecution pointed that out as well, and rightly so. Namely, that we have to be extremely cautious when identifying somebody in order not to harm somebody, especially not one of the accused. Witness P-030 was perhaps misled by the movie called 100 Days of Vukovar when a different person was shown and the name Miroslav Radic was constantly attributed to that person, and that was a different person in that footage. Perhaps Witness P-030 had to state that before the Trial Chamber because, and we mustn't forget that he was one of the persons that was subjected to special investigation by Croatian secret police, SIS. I think that Exhibit 300 deals with this. This exhibit was adduced. And let me repeat here that this secret Croatian service managed to acquire information, secret information, from this OTP, and OTP should be concerned about this. They used this information in order to prepare some witnesses, including Witness P-030, and naturally somebody had to confirm the allegations in this hastily assembled indictment. They didn't manage to do this in the end. I think that the Prosecution should have attempted to word the prosecution in a different way and the aim of that indictment should have been to establish the truth and ensure a fair trial. Another allegation of the Prosecution has to do with selection and boarding on buses. On the 20th of November according to the Prosecution in view of everything that I have stated so far, Radic was together with Sljivacanin at the hospital. The Prosecution says yes, but in a different context. And we could have avoided this, because we knew the factual situation. Radic said the truth when he said that he was at the hospital, but he went there later after the evacuation. He wore camouflage uniform. He did not meet Sljivacanin. He wasn't present during triage, selection, and escorting of the people to buses. The Prosecution invokes the testimony of Witness P-018 who said that he went with Radic to the hospital perhaps, but in that case the Trial Chamber here has to believe Witness Radic, because a number of persons I mentioned confirmed that Radic was not present during the evacuation, and I think that this is what we should highlight. On the other hand, if we only remember the testimony of Witness P-002 and 022, we will see that these two witnesses spoke about (redacted) (redacted) in order to see what was happening at the hospital. Witness P-002 stated here, when testifying, that upon arriving at the hospital he did not see Miroslav Radic. He knows him well, and he tried hard to aggravate his position in the trial. P-022 claims that Captain Radic was with Petrova Gora and he sent him to take P-002 to the hospital. At the very moment when P-002 and P-022 were at the hospital, Radic was elsewhere altogether. The witnesses we heard here and the witnesses questioned in detail by the OTP told us about the process of the search, selection, and triage. It was our understanding when looking at the rules that some of that business or the involvement of the military security in some of the business or the involvement of the military police, it would have been so illogical and so lifeless to reach the conclusion that an ordinary captain of an ordinary military police company in a complicated operation like this simply strolled along in order to issue orders to members of the military police and the security organ. As for Radic's presence at the barracks in relation to Witness P-030, the one and only witness causing a lot of harm to Miroslav Radic because of these two arbitrary constructions that he put together, Witness P-030 says that, again after a while, he saw Captain Radic in the barracks, this time, however, wearing some sort of a leather jacket and a Bordeaux dark red colour beret, a cap that would not have been worn by any officer, let alone Radic. He said he was holding a list of names and searching persons who were later taken or, rather, returned to the hospital. Another witness we heard was the accused Sljivacanin's deputy, Ljubisa Vukasinovic. Vukasinovic says, "I am the one who put persons on the buses. I am the one who took 15 people off the buses inside the barracks according to a list that I had and sent those back to the hospital." This was his duty. This was his mission. He was asked directly if Captain Miroslav Radic had any part in this or indeed if he had ever been seen at the barracks. The answer was a clear negative. Witness Susic was heard as well. He exercised command over the military police at the barracks. He never met or laid eyes on Captain Radic in the barracks, not before this time, not at the critical time. I'm not sure how to phrase this mildly. There is this attempt by the OTP to perhaps speculate, I'm not sure if that makes any sense, but I'm an at a loss for a better word. As for Vukosinovic's evidence and the evidence of Witness P-030, those are not mutually exclusive they say because Vukosinovic looked at three buses. There is obviously the possibility that Radic looked at some other buses, they say. Vukosinovic is crystal clear on this. "I'm the one." These people are honourable witnesses who testified under oath causing themselves a lot of grief. He says, "I'm the one who read the names off that list, took people off that bus, and sent them back to the hospital." There is no dilemma involved here. There is no possible interpretation that can possibly aggravate the position of Miroslav Radic. Bearing all of this in mind, and we did try to explain this in some detail in our final brief, it is perfectly clear that Radic could not possibly have been present when people were mistreated or beaten in the hospital, in the barracks, or, for that matter, at a later time, if indeed such a thing ever occurred within the hospital compound, within the perimeter of the hospital. He could not have been involved in the so-called reselection that occur later on at the hospital as posited by the OTP in their final brief, in the presence of Miroljub Vujevic, a TO member, which means that he could never have known since he wasn't there, that the prisoners had been attacked or threatened in any way. I think the evidence is self-explanatory and the Defence does not have the slightest doubt about this. As for the mistreatment and killings at Ovcara on the 20th of November, this is something that the OTP addressed. The Defence denied this from day one, denied Radic's involvement in any way. Radic never found out, and I will address the issue more thoroughly at a later stage. There is a special chapter dedicated by the OTP to the omission of the Guards Motorised Brigade to intervene in the more effective way during the evacuation of the hospital and the withdrawal from Ovcara later on. I think Mr. Vasic addressed that in quite some length. This is about the responsibility of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade. The Radic Defence believes the following: This is a very serious circumstance and Defence counsel, in any criminal case, find it very difficult to say this. But the Prosecution have clear evidence against certain people from the 80th Kragujevac Brigade. And I'm saying this, not because I now wish to cause grief, any grief at all to someone else, but because those people decided to side with the OTP. They're trying to now glorify their own actions there at the time and some of these people occupy very high-ranking positions in what used to be the army of Yugoslavia and is now the army of Serbia. Whereas what I have here is a petty captain who left the army back in 1992 and he was on a fast track to a glittering military career yet decided to leave. Now he's supposed to foot the bill for these omissions committed by people who had to take better care of their own zone of responsibility. Vujnovic was the town commander for Jakupovac, Ovcara, and Grabovo, all three locations. His own man was the commander of Ovcara, a responsibility which he had bestowed on him, and at the time in question, he was there. He witnessed the mistreatment and the attacks. They had the knowledge. They had the awareness that a crime might happen at Ovcara, but they ran. They ran at 2230 hundred hours that night. They simply got away. In addition to running from the scene at 2230 hundred hours, and in addition to saying that no crime had occurred before then, this is directly denied by Witness P-022, who says that the crimes actually took place between 1700 hours and later on. And he says he left for Petrova Gora at 11, 12, or 1.00. If we respect the principle in dubio pro reo, which means that in that case we have to favour the accused, we to have lend credence to the theory that he was at Petrova Gora at 11.00 on the 20th of November. If, at 11.00, he was there and he doesn't know exactly how he got from Petrova Gora back to Ovcara, which is what he says, then we have to believe that he simply walked there, which means he had left a lot earlier before the 80th Kragujevac Brigade abandoned Ovcara, before Ovcara was abandoned by Witness P-022. Therefore, he could not have known that a crime was in progress and was not himself involved. At any rate, I will be addressing the issue, but especially later on. In theory, that Radic had to leave with his company after 11.00 with his company, in order to foil the killings is entirely unfounded. Firstly, he didn't know what Witness P-022 claims he knew. Secondly, this is the area of responsibility covered by the 80th Kragujevac Motorised Brigade. They have their own military police company. He had no business calling them over to their area of responsibility. This theory is entirely unfounded and I'm not even sure what it stems from. One thing we mustn't forget is this: If at 10.30 on the 20th of November, they ran, they abandoned the area where the crime occurred, on the 21st of November at 0600 hours, in the OTP's submission, and we have that in evidence, the Vukovar TO was resubordinated to the 80th Kragujevac Brigade. Okay, 10.30, the time between 10.30 and 6.00 the following morning, they were still at Ovcara in the yellow house because that's where the town commander was, the Ovcara town commander. They assumed responsibility de jure at 6.00 that morning. They were the ones who were in a position to stop that crime from happening firstly and, secondly, to -- to punish the Vukovar TO members because it was de jure that they were resubordinated to them at 0600 hours on the 21st of November, that morning, therefore, these two major counts of the indictment are easily challenged and they invoke the responsibility of Captain Miroslav Radic. The next important question is whether the crimes at Ovcara were predictable. This is an important question for the Trial Chamber. The OTP believes that the accused should have known about the reputation of the TO for lawlessness. The OTP corroborates this by saying that the JNA people had the duty to be informed about their own respective areas of responsibility and their subordinates. Not a single company commander actually has a zone of responsibility according to the doctrine. They can act in concert in coordination. It is only from the battalion level up that areas of responsibility are assigned and I think even the OTP experts confirmed this. However, at the time when Radic was along the axis of operations of his own company, not a single crime took place, even in a layman's interpretation, which is to say, that it was some sort of area of responsibility, meaning the location along the axis of operations of his company. Radic's blamed even for things that he did well, in the sense of him being aware of the poor reputation of the TO, because Miroslav Radic was involved in the fighting along the front line. This is entirely unfounded. He was an honourable officer. He fought. He didn't shy away from the fighting. He didn't hide in the surrounding villages such as Negoslavci as some officers did. He was there. He stuck with his soldiers. We heard evidence from people who were wounded at the front line how he looked after them after the war. All of that was misused by the OTP. Even Radic visiting the graves of some of the people who were killed, it is quite clear he didn't know, even if some of those people had been involved, why would he have visited them. This proves his innocence if it proves anything at all. Another thing about this, about Radic being aware of the reputation, of the poor reputation of the TO is this: The OTP talks about his friendship with Karanfilov. Incredible. I never found anything about that. I've gone through all the transcripts. What the OTP could possibly have had in mind, so my conclusion was this: Miroslav Radic himself was in Negoslavci once in October back when he was wounded and that's in evidence and then twice on the 13th and 14th of November when he came there to get permission, authorisation that was to be signed by Momcilovic for leave, extra leave awarded to him by Captain Stijakovic, the commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion as a reward. I have gone through all the transcripts. There is nothing, nothing at all to indicate that he and Karanfilov if indeed they ever met at all and there is no evidence to show that, that he and Karanfilov discussed the problems and the lawlessness of the Vukovar TO. Therefore, these two conditionally speaking attempts by the OTP to blame Miroslav Radic for this led to nothing in my submission. As for the behaviour of the Vukovar TO prior to the 18th of November, 1991, paragraph 178 we see this wording again, namely that the Vukovar TO members were subordinated to Radic and that he accepted their reputation -- the reputation of the TO and the volunteers in his interview, an interview which has been exhibited and I will be addressing that later. However these two are entirely erroneous premises which the OTP have used as a foundation for their theory firstly the fact that these people were subordinated to Radic and we shall prove by the end of our closing argument that in fact they weren't. In our final brief and through our case I think we have even succeeded in convincing the OTP to a significant degree at least. The thing is we heard about this interview given by Miroslav Radic that he trained, as the interview claims, nearly 500 people but we also heard a witness who was the chief of security of the 80 Kragujevac Brigade whose last name is Vukosavljevic. He says that about 400 people from the 1st battalion or the 2nd of the 80 Kragujevac Motorised Brigade I'm not quite sure at the very outset actually found themselves in the Petrova Gora area. They were securing the area. They were enjoying some sort of logistical support but they weren't at the actual front line and it is in relation to them that Captain Radic is claiming that they were some of the volunteers which at the stage one of the operation he helped to train. Therefore these are not Vukovar TO members. These are volunteers from Serbia, and unfortunately there were some of those in the area too. The fact about indiscipline and Radic is this is not in relation to TO. This is in relation to the volunteers. This tells us many things. This first of all favours Radic as someone who had established a good command climate which is again abused by the OTP on the other hand he identified all of those who were a potential source of trouble. Therefore, those who remained were not people who had criminal reputations of any kind and there was nothing to suggest that those people would suggest crimes. Unfortunately the Prosecution invokes Witness P-024 who is a witness that I invoked at the outset. I said this witness had to be prosecuted because of all the things that he did not only in Serbia but also because of perjury that he committed before this Trial Chamber. He says that there was a lack of discipline among Radic's men that there was violence and that there was a generally known principle at the time. All of the witnesses including P-022, P-018, OTP witnesses as well as all the officers and soldiers that we heard throughout this trial are unanimous in this. Radic was an honourable officer a serious officer a strict officer and an honest officer. There is no doubt about this. Trifunovic of all people spoke about this when questioned by the Defence about the command climate. All of it in relation to evidence provided by OTP experts before this Trial Chamber. Why was P-024 assigned this kind of role? Well, the Defence is at a loss. This is the greatest Tribunal of this kind in the world and our belief is that credible witnesses should be brought before this Tribunal. Witness P-024, I am not using his evidence. I am not abusing the patience of this Court. But when we suggested he be prosecuted, the decision was made that the Chamber would take into consideration everything that we submitted in terms of documents when deciding on the credibility of this particular witness, which means that I now have to remind the Chamber that this witness was unfamiliar with fundamental concepts relating to the area in which he was at the time. He said that in addition to the Leva Supoderica Detachment there was the Desna Supoderica Detachment. Nonsense we won't forget the notebook, the booklet, a photocopy of which he brought along for his testimony which was a piece of forgery as simple as that. Thirdly -- or, rather, on page 3 of the document there's a box where you need to get stamp for the military post and there were some general stamps there belonging to a local commune, some local commune rather, and I think we used Witness Trifunovic to disprove that. We then asked him about the original of that booklet. We can't possibly use a photocopy as evidence in a trial such as this, especially if that is the only thing that corroborates this document. And he simply said that he had burned it. Why then did we seek that this witness be criminally prosecuted. We showed him Exhibit 19 A. He said that at the time he would meet Captain Radic on a daily basis as well as his own captain Kameni. That he was his right-hand man virtually and we showed him that photograph Exhibit 19 A and he simply failed to recognise his own commander in that photograph which can only suggest that he lied to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My learned friends failed to do a background check on him and see that he -- that he was a convicted criminal. That says -- that speaks volumes about his credibility. In paragraph 100 -- it 283, the Prosecutor speaks about violence. They speak about the beatings outside Radic's command post and the kills and beatings that took place across the road in a house, as suggested by Witness P-018. That's where there was a detention facility. That's what he says. So this was the theory put forward by the OTP. P-018 claimed that there was this special building. As concerns the Defence of Miroslav Radic, we asked all the witnesses this very question even Witness P-022. In this street at Petrova Gora was there any sort of detention facility or a house where people were tortured? There wasn't a single witness to confirm that. Quite the contrary. The witnesses were astonished to hear about this fabrication. Witness P-018, at any rate we cross-examine him, he said that at Ovcara 1.040 people were killed he was he was there. The transcript reference is 7564, 7565. However -- however, he also says that he was furious, that he made up these statements as he went along. He denied ever having been present at Ovcara and so on and so forth. The Prosecution is submitting something that is entirely erroneous and my learned young friend Mr. Lunny spoke about that yesterday, namely that Radic was present when a Croatian POW was beaten by the Vukovar TO. This is a fabrication that has been repeated many times. The witness invoked is Witness P-022. The Defence claims and this is easy enough to prove, that this was no Croatian POW at all to begin with. Secondly, even according to the submissions of Witness P-022 he wasn't in fact beaten by the TO or the Leva Supoderica men but which the military policemen securing Tesic's headquarters. This is the notorious addendum made by Witness P-022 -- the addendum which additionally appeared just on the eve of his evidence here, 15 years later he remembers that a man was beaten up and that Captain Miroslav Radic was cool as a cucumber, never raised a finger. This was probably to back up his own false allegation that when people came from Ovcara and told him about the crime he just shrugged his shoulders. Why are we so convinced that this is perjury, that this is false evidence? It is for the following reason Witness P-022, in the transcript on page 4979/19, this witness says about this person who the OTP claim was a Croatian POW beaten by members of the TO, "Radic told me to take him to Major Tesic's HQ which I did. There were military policemen there and I said this is a deserter, whereupon one of the military policemen struck out at Krstic. Krstic hit him in the head, in fact. He then fell down and was beaten by another four persons... I then went back to the headquarters and reported this to Captain Radic." It is based on this that you can see this was no Croatian POW and was not beaten by the TO members. Thereafter, on page T 5100/16 he said, "I, Radic, and Vidic saw that and we watched it." So even in this construction there was no reference to Miroslav Radic's being at the command post and he was not being beaten by TO members. Witness P-022, in connection with the Krstic case, as we called it, to the question whether that had happened on the very same day when Lieutenant Kostic had died in transcript 0999/4 says, "Yes," because it was on the same day and only eight -- eight lines further on page 5099/16 he says "No." After all, I'm not going to belabour the point. It is the position of the Defence that this witness misinterpreted things proceeding from misinterpretation of the military orders that were presented and also that the testimony of this witness -- do I have more time before the break? I'm not able to tell. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: The break should be around about now. We had until five past, so you can go for a few minutes or if -- can we have the break now or...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can have the break now. Thank you. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: We will start again at five to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The next question is Seselj's visit to which the Prosecution attaches more importance than I consider is warranted for the problem that we have at hand in this courtroom and to his -- and his visit on the 13th of November, as the Prosecution puts it to Radic's command post. Radic did not have a command post, that we heard many times already. The witness never actually said so in his note which we presented as evidence and that note it is very interesting because we waited for 15 years to appear before a Court, because that witness had taken the stand in many other cases, and I'm not going to say which in order not to reveal his identity. There is a formulation there by Seselj to the effect that no Ustasha can leave Vukovar alive. That is the way it was interpreted. Until that note, that memo appeared and analysing it we actually ascertained that what was written there was no Ustasha can get out, but there is another formulation which says no volunteer can -- may leave Vukovar. So that is another one there. So by a compilation of these -- JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: I'm sorry, Mr. Borovic, but I don't see in the transcript a reference to the witness that you are referring to. You may have said it, but I don't see it, or I overlooked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will -- I was referring to the Witness P-022, and his document which was led here as evidence. P-022 is the witness. I shall just say that the note makes no reference whatsoever to a command post. What it does make reference to is the house of so-and-so. In the note, and that was presented as a piece of evidence, 884, page 212, the name of Captain Radic is not mentioned as the person attending the meeting whereas it would have been logical for his name to have been jotted down along with the other ones. This witness tried to invoke colleagues Peternik and Prelic who gave testimony before the court in Belgrade when the Defence stated that they had -- when the Defence actually said that to them, to him, what they had said, the only thing that he had to say is that these were insane people, crazy people, and liars. However, what is of importance for this Court, we have dealt with it in the trial brief, so that I'm not going to go into detail but just the essentials. On page 2005, the note says, "(redacted) is coming. He's arriving. He is wounded." The witness Razvigor Virijevic, Mladen Maric, Milivoje Simic, and Jovan Susic, and -- were asked by me whether officer (redacted) had ever been wounded at the Vukovar front and they all denied that. Then most interesting, which also undermines the credibility of that alleged document is the part which is on page 199 of the notebook and I should like to ask the Bench to take a good look at page 199 as well as page 200 and that for the following reason: Because it shows that this witness P-002, to whom greater importance is attached indeed, actually inserted on page 200 Captain Radic without any context, and then he subsequently added in a different pencil colour the name of Captain Radic. He talks about the axis of operations where captain (redacted) is and the captain -- the tank operator Ristic who he called Rile, and then on page 200, after this name Rile, he just added in parenthesis Radic, and then Rile is an abbreviation for Ristic. It is short for Ristic and Rile is short for Radic. So obviously there was no mistake, but by subsequently later fabricating this note, he inserted him in that particular period 13th of November, while at that time, Radic was actually in Negoslavci and that was the time when he went to Belgrade to get that permit. In our final brief, we submitted an analysis of all that he had written there, and worst of all and to which the Prosecution -- in the fact that the Prosecution devotes so much attention to this witness is that this witness came to this Prosecution either of his own volition or initiative or I don't know why and with the courtesy of our colleagues he gave – (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) people who come to give false statements for money and at a certain time were ardent followers and servants of the regime of Slobodan Milosevic. Well, I have to say that in 1991, in March, we were on opposite sides. I was at the helm of the biggest opposition party in Serbia, and he was on the other side. So this is something that the public has to know because those riots, those demonstrations were the largest ones organised after the war because of the writings in the regime's media and this person wrote for one of the regime's papers. I'm not going to say which. So five years later, after he had learned, as he says, of the crimes of the 21st of November, and it had been his duty to report that but he hadn't, but he waited for five or six years and then started concocting the scenario in agreement with the OTP. As regards the knowledge of the accused of the behaviour of the Territorial Defence on the 18th and 19th of November, I shall try to be brief. He said that Radic attended the evacuation from the hospital. He claimed that patients in light blue striped pyjamas all clean-shaven and very neat were all taken out. Dr. Vesna Bosanac didn't say -- didn't know that the wounded and the sick had been dressed in that fashion, and she confirmed that the army had first entered the hospital compound on the 19th of November, 1991, and this was confirmed by P-021, 20 -- 2D04, Paunovic, Simic, and other witnesses. We should not forget when the colleague from the Defence team of Mr. Sljivacanin showed the argument between Sljivacanin and Borsinger on the 20th of November, the witness, without batting an eyelash, said in court that that had been a few days before that in Belgrade. He actually lied, because he didn't know how to explain about Captain Radic, in what unit he was or where he was, nor did he provide any evidence about what he wrote. And when he was asked, on a map, Exhibit 156, to show where the hospital was in Vukovar, he was unable to do so. And he actually testified here to the fact that he was a psychiatric patient but did not use drugs but discarded them. And then when we pressurised him with proof that the actual evacuation was on the 20th of November and when we showed him the photograph of the soldier, it was quite clear that this witness did not know at all what had happened in Vukovar on that day. And as he said, "I was with the JNA and someone is going to pay dearly for everything that happened to me." And I believe that this is a position that is not to be adopted by any witness who is to give evidence before this Court. Three, the knowledge of the accused about the conduct of the Territorial Defence on the 20th of November, 1991, and this refers to abuses and mistreatment of people. Actually, what happened in the hospital and the barracks. And as I have presented the Defence's position, I'm not going to go into detail. As regards the knowledge of the Guards Motorised Brigade on crimes, the OTP invokes P-022 and P-018, the witnesses, namely, that Captain Radic had found out from witnesses what had happened, that he had found out what had happened. He just shrugged his shoulders, said they, Captain Radic, according to him, was actually in the next room and could be -- was able to hear what was being said. The Defence managed to prove that Witness P-022, who is the most important witness in respect of this fact, according to the OTP, was lying, was not telling the truth owing to this fact. He actually gave his statement to the OTP as a suspect. He was told, "You are a suspect but there will be no criminal proceedings instituted against you."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to just quote something he said to demonstrate that on the 20th of November, at the critical time when the crimes took place, he was not at Ovcara, irrespective of the fact that he -- he claims that he was a killer and that he was at Ovcara. He said that the security of Captain Radic took P-022 to hospital. He claims that on the orders of Captain Radic he took Witness P-002 to the hospital, and he was asked how long he stayed in the hospital, and then he said "about one hour. Following that, I returned back to the headquarters, and on that day, Your Honours, I remained within the staff sector." Various dates were mentioned there, when it comes to the bringing of Witness P-002 by Witness P-022 to the hospital, but what is the most important for this Tribunal is that both of them stated that he was brought to the hospital only once with the assistance of soldier P-022. We went over what was supplied by the OTP, and we found video footage, Exhibit 568 in this trial, and in that film, in that excerpt, we can see Witness P-002 at the time of the evacuation. I may have made a mistake concerning protected witnesses. I am doing my best, Your Honours. All of them are protected witnesses with a P and multiple 0s. Exhibit 568. If both witnesses claim that they met only on that day and were brought to the hospital only on that day, and Witness P-022 claims that Captain Radic remained at home or, rather, at Petrova Gora, and that he returned and spent the entire day in the sector of the headquarters, that is to say, Petrova Gora, then he could not have been at Ovcara at 12.00 as he claimed here to the Trial Chamber. What remains for us to do? We believe that this Trial Chamber consisting of professional Judges should not allow, and I'm sure that they will not allow themselves to believe this witness who was a blackmailed witness without verifying the facts. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If we were now to try and verify the claims of this witness concerning other two soldiers, it would be a futile attempt. The persons that he mentioned as being at Ovcara were Jankovic and Vidacek. Both of those witnesses are dead now and it's not a coincidence in my view the fact that he decided to mention two persons who cannot support or discredit his story, and by doing so he denied us the possibility to believe him that following the crimes that he committed he went back to Nova Street and told Captain Radic about the events at Ovcara. Why shouldn't we believe him is fully -- is further supported by the fact that he doesn't know when he came back, with whom he came back, and what his most surprising is that he says he was in civilian clothes with a rifle that wasn't a standard issue rifle. Witness P-002 was asked the following: On that day, the 22nd of November, when this witness that we are referring to now brought him to the hospital, how he was dressed and what weapons he had, he confirmed what he stated in the Belgrade Ovcara trial, namely that he had a camouflage uniform, an M-72 automatic rifle on him. On the same day at the same time that we're referring to now I think that in this instance Witness P-002 should be believed. We heard from Witness P-022 that he killed in front of the hangar from 1700 hours onwards. He said that there was a hall in front of the hangar, and there is not another witness who was at Ovcara whom I failed to ask, including the colonel who conducted sanitization following the war, whether any traces of a hall in front of the entrance into hangar were found, and this colonel said very graphically, "No. I only saw soil."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly apologise. Can we move into private session, please. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are -- we're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Witness P-018, we brought witnesses Stijakovic, Vuckovic, Zirojevic, and Tesic to contradict him, because during the critical evening Radic on the 20th evening attended dinner at Vuckovic's. It is true, and later on I will speak about this. For the second time Witness P-002 spoke the truth. Contrary to Witness P-022, he said on the 20th of November in the evening he was at home with Nada and Stanko and that evening Radic did not come home. As for the 21st of November and what Witness P-002 told us about that, from the note we were able to establish that there never existed any command post. Rather, there was a house, Nada and Stanko's home, and this witness never asked Captain Radic directly about murders at Ovcara. In cross-examination when we cornered him specifically about what he had asked Captain Radic, he answered, "Well, that." "Question: What that?" This is not something that could be taken as serious indication that he truly asked Captain Radic about what had happened at Ovcara. Following that, we tried to verify his claims and he provided three versions to us. Number one, that he asked him at the same time as Stanko. Then the second version was that he asked him later on when he met him in passing no less. And the third version was that he thought that it was either that evening or the following evening. When comes to such an important fact, we are not convinced, we do not have evidence that proves beyond reasonable doubt that he indeed asked Captain Radic about it, especially since we provided evidence to the Trial Chamber that on the 21st of November Radic had an inspection of his company conducted by Stijakovic deputy commander of the 1st Motorised Battalion. This is further proven by Zirojevic, Stojanovic, Vuckovic and Stijakovic naturally. This witness attempted to show us that he spoke the truth, and he even offered to confirm this in writing, and he invoked two witnesses to support this. One was the volunteer Daca, and the other one was Slavisa Pavlovic from Smederevo. Your Honours, this is a tried and trusted recipe used by false witnesses. He again attempts to rely on two dead persons. We cannot verify whether he indeed spoke to these people. Both of them are dead. When we cross-examined him about his notes, especially about Slavisa Pavlovic, we asked him when he wrote down the name of Slavisa Pavlovic. Witness P-002 said, "I wrote that in later on because Aleksandar Vasiljevic told me the name of that person." Do you see the absurdity of this, namely, that the general of Yugoslav People's Army told him the name of a volunteer from Smederevo five years after the fact, and he never saw this person. Can the Court really rely on this? And what is the worst thing about this witness, which undermines his credibility, is that he made a lot of notations later on and then corrected them. We spoke about this in our final brief. And when it comes to the crimes at Ovcara, it says that he asked Stanko, "Why didn't you do this in a more discreet way?" Can you believe the attitude of this witness, who in 1991, approved a crime that was committed against innocent people by asking, Why didn't you do it in a more discreet way? He never reported this to anyone, and then later on he moved to an opposition paper. Why did he do it? Because he wanted to make money. That idea occurred to him. He lied, and somebody will be held responsible for this, I hope. Now I will speak about the responsibility of the accused, because this is of greater interest to the Trial Chamber than the issues that I spoke of just now. If we are dealing with joint criminal enterprise -- now that we're dealing with joint criminal enterprise, Your Honours, the Prosecution claims that Mrksic, Radic, Sljivacanin together with other members of the joint criminal enterprise had a plan to persecute Croats and other non-Serbs present in the Vukovar Hospital. They list three things, three points which I'll link to this Prosecution plan. Number one, that Mrksic designated Sljivacanin as the person in charge of the evacuation of the hospital; two, that the evacuation was conducted before the arrival of international observers; and three, and this is something to do with my client, namely, that the triage and selection were conducted with the assistance of Radic, officer of the Guards Motorised Brigade. Your Honours, Miroslav Radic did not participate in creating any sort of a plan nor did he participate in selection, search or triage. This is something that witnesses Sljivancanin, Simic, Paunovic, Vukasinovic, and Karan speak about. The Prosecution claims that the crimes were within the objective of joint criminal enterprise and that each of the accused had intention to carry out these crimes, or one of the crimes. The Prosecution believes that there had to be joint act, and that is true, but other participants of joint criminal enterprise listed by the Prosecution, specifically, Miroslav Radic as company commander had no joint action with any other members of joint criminal enterprise as defined by the Prosecution. He had no plan involving members of the Vukovar TO, nor did he in any way share the intention to execute that plan, to implement it. I regret the fact that some honest witnesses testified here and told the truth and the Prosecution misinterpreted that in their final brief. The joint plan was to persecute Croats, and crimes for which Miroslav Radic is charged with are part of that plan. Now the Prosecution are saying, if they were not part to a joint plan, then alternatively it was foreseeable and that Radic took the risk or accepted the risk. However, I'm now repeating myself, and I'm doing that only because in the OTP final brief, these issues mention several times. He was not present at the hospital during the evacuation. He did not go to the barracks at all, and he was not at Ovcara at all. So it is quite clear that he could not have persecuted Croats. He had no joint plan, no joint action, and that he wasn't able to carry out murders, torture, inhumane treatment, or treating inhumanely prisoners at the hospital, in the barracks, and Ovcara. It is quite clear that in the alternative of what the Prosecution is saying, if there was no joint plan, Radic wasn't able either to foresee what was going to happen, nor did he voluntarily accept to participate in the crime. As for the earlier plan concept, the one mentioned by the Prosecution, in order for the joint plan to materialise, there need not be previous preparation, and this can stem from some facts. Theoretically, this is true. However, the Prosecution claims that the first steps aimed at persecuting Croats, torturing and killing prisoners, began before the 19th and 20th of November, 1991. They mostly speak about the status of Sljivacanin and Mrksic in that regard and devote less intention to Radic. As for the Territorial Defence of Vukovar and members of the joint criminal enterprise, I will speak very briefly about that because I will devote most of my attention to what the Prosecution insisted on most, namely, that they were subordinated to Captain Miroslav Radic which is not true. So the status and participation in joint criminal enterprise is not something that is of interest to the defence of Miroslav Radic. The Prosecution claims that Radic and units subordinated to him contributed to the commission of the crime. Why did I say that I wasn't going to speak of this in detail? Because the Prosecution keeps saying that Radic and units subordinated to him participated in triage, and then that Radic was seen at the barracks together with Sljivacanin and that he sent at least three soldiers to Ovcara. Radic's intention to work together with the co-accused and other members of the joint criminal enterprise in order to achieve the joint plan and goal boils down to triage and beating of the people in the barracks and at the hospital, and then they go on to say that Radic was aware of this beating and torture. We deny this fully, and we base this on the facts that we pointed out during our case and the fact that he wasn't present in these places at the time. It is said that Radic omitted to act when the three soldiers got back, that's the third circumstance. And he was aware of this goal, and he was aware of the secret evacuation. They said units were never subordinate to Radic. It is the position of our Defence that Radic never sent any soldiers to Ovcara and therefore he could not have been aware of the killing or the beating that took place at Ovcara. The OTP also states that the international observers were banned from entering the hospital. My colleagues have addressed that, and I won't be repeating it. What is important for this context, speaking of the knowledge of the accused, any knowledge that the accused may have had of the violent behaviour by the TO prior to the hospital evacuation, the OTP claims that Radic should have known about this information from the 1st Military District because according to the chain of command he should have found out from Tesic, but we have seen no evidence to corroborate this. Again there is a reference there to his friendship with Karanfilov. They had spent four years together at the military academy, but they weren't the only ones. There were plenty of friendships there. So this is an encounter -- or, rather, this meeting where the TO was supposed to be discussed never materialised. It's as simple as that. As far as his involvement in the joint plan is concerned, for the most part the OTP rely on the briefing in Negoslavci on that day. So if that's the case it's quite obvious, isn't it, that Radic, if he was involved in the joint criminal enterprise at least he would have turned up at that meeting in Negoslavci where Mrksic was present, Sljivacanin and everybody else who made up the command structure so to speak. The Prosecution is trying to -- to sort of pin on Mr. Radic that he was in Negoslavci at least that once or twice when he went there to get the permit so that they may be able to place him in the context of knowledge of the plan in some way. Radic did not additionally contribute to that plan since he didn't know, and therefore he could not have been involved in the selection at the hospital. He could not have been in the barracks. He could not have seen what happened there. He didn't know about the government meeting. He was never at Ovcara. And I think the Defence has been successful in proving this. My learned friends addressed in a particular way the question of intent. Intent is something that matters a lot in this legal framework. They said that the accused shared a joint intent, and then again there are allegations that Radic participated in the beatings on the 18th of November, that he was involved in the selection process at the barracks and in the hospital. Some witnesses are named. However, the OTP have never succeeded in proving that Radic had an awareness of this to begin with, and nobody reported to him. There was talk of three soldiers, but he never sent anyone there to begin with. I'm not dealing with this any more because this is very repetitive and it's all about three particular circumstances and three places where Radic had no role to play, leaving him allegedly in this really serious story. But since the OTP have provided no serious evidence, I won't be dwelling on this individual criminal responsibility 7(1) and 7(3). Radic was aware of the threats being made to prisoners. He was aware of the reputation, and he was able to predict what would happen. That's what the Prosecution claims when quoting P-016 and the alleged statement made by Radic "These are dead men." But the timing is not right and the witness cannot trusted. Therefore, Radic's awareness is not corroborated. That is our submission. Therefore, Radic could not have prevented any mistreatment in the barracks in the hospital or at Ovcara itself. As to the actus reus, in relation to 7(1), the OTP claims that Radic aided and abetted the principal perpetrators of the crime by being involved in the mistreatment in taking victims away from the hospital and being involved in the selection process in the barracks and again we're back to square one, these issues of responsibility. Radic is aiding the principal perpetrators and then there is special focus given to the selection process to him aiding Sljivacanin with the selection process. There is a reference to Njavro, to Anto Aric and the Defence believes that none of this requires any further comments at all. In terms of individual responsibility, Article 7(1) cannot even exist. Radic was not involved in the reselection in the JNA barracks. As for the theory that Radic allowed regular soldiers to be involved in the crimes at Ovcara. Well, even if we look at the evidence of that particular witness, there is nothing to indicate that he could possibly have had this sort of intent or for that matter an awareness of what might happen at Ovcara even if you take that statement, even if you see it in the most favourable light, it can't be used as evidence to show this, and it must be proved beyond reasonable doubt which it wasn't. It has not been that Radic was involved in a joint criminal enterprise or indeed that there was some sort of coordinated cooperation between them as co-perpetrators. By this very fact we have to address the question of mens rea about Radic knowing that by his acts and omissions he was contributing to the joint criminal enterprise. This is not true. Radic was not in the hospital. He was not in the barracks. He was not familiar with the criminal propensity of the main perpetrators. He was not involved in the selection process in the hospital. He was not involved in the mistreatment on the 18th of November. He was not present in the barracks when those 20 people were taken off that bus. He had no intention of committing any sort of acts of discrimination along any ethnic, religious or racial lines -- no discrimination whatsoever. Nor have the OTP been able to prove anything at all to that effect. The OTP have not succeeded in proving that the accused had the sufficient mens rea in terms of knowing that his own actions would contribute to the commission of a crime or indeed that he was aware of the exceptional likelihood that his own actions might contribute to the commission of a crime. As for Article 7(3), we're speaking here about effective control. This is a very important issue. The OTP claims there was both de jure and de facto control. The Defence took issue with that -- that Captain Radic had effective control over the TO on the Leva Supoderica Detachment. I would like to particularly draw your attention to the 10th of November, 1991. The OTP had the ambition obviously in their final brief and I must address this specially to use legal and doctrinal documents to invoke certain witnesses in relation to this issue of effective control. Above all as for any legal and doctrinal regulations, such as ones invoked by the OTP, we would like to say this: It is certainly true that in Yugoslavia and in the SFRY that is, there were such legal and doctrinal regulations that existed quite independently of the influence of Miroslav Radic but he as a company commander was duty-bound to apply those. Secondly, in the armed forces of the SFRY there was a well-established system of control and command. This existed quite independently from any influence potentially exercised by Miroslav Radic. He was duty-bound to comply with that system, the system already in place. Radic was sent to Vukovar. There was nothing he could have done about that. There was nothing he could have done about the mission given to the Guards Motorised Brigade, the 1st Motorised Brigade and his own 3rd Motorised Company. Facts have been proved beyond doubt if we look at the OTP witnesses and the Defence Witness Forca. The following facts: The TO was organised from the lowest possible level and then up to the republican level. There was the municipal TO, municipal Vukovar TO at a certain point in time. It split up into the Serbian faction and the Croat faction. The Serb faction was the one that -- or rather, the Croat faction was the one favouring secession from the SFRY and not in favour of siding with the JNA in order to preserve the unity of Yugoslavia. What has been proved as a fact is that a TO detachment is the highest-ranking unit of the TO within its territorial structure. Expert Theunens should know that this is a huge force in terms of manoeuvring power to be employed in a small area like that. The existence of the TO is beyond doubt even prior to the arrival of the Guards Motorised Brigade in Vukovar, Your Honours. This is confirmed by a written order on lifting the blockade and attacking Exhibit 405 issued by the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade, Mrksic, the 1st of October 1991. If you look at item 3 of that order there's reference there to neighbours. There's a store called the Vukovar Territorial Defence who were neighbours. They had four companies. They had good equipment. They were armed and they had their own logistic support. The rules of combat, rules of engagement that prevailed in the JNA and I think this is very important for our purposes are the rules in relation to the battalions, platoons and companies and these rules say in no uncertain terms which unit can be used to reinforce which other unit within the structure of the JNA, which unit is used to reinforce which other unit in the JNA. And then if you look at the rules in relation to the company and platoon and in relation to motorised companies all it says is that there could have been an element from that company, a platoon specifically, and this could have been reinforced by a unit of the Territorial Defence but not a company in its entirety. It was not possible for an entire TO detachment to be attached to a company. That was out of the question. As for the established system of control and command and the OTP expert says it was almost at NATO level that it was very good and well-established. It's very easy to conclude that within that system of command Mrksic and all the other superior commanders were familiar with the provisions of this rule. They knew full well which units could be attached to which other units and this rule was very much applied in everyday practice. As for temporary units, temporary formations such as Operations Group Assault Detachment and Assault Group there is no doctrinal rule among those invoked by the OTP saying that a company could be used in the role of an assault group. There is no rule anywhere to suggest that possibility. At any rate let's try to imagine a single street in Vukovar where operations were in progress. There were buildings, there were streets. The witness told us all of that. You couldn't fit a company into that one street with a Territorial Defence Detachment attached. There could have been only one group. This is settled area after all teeming with houses. As for command of the armed forces in the SFRY what is accepted there is the right to decide to give orders and to exercise control. A person is appointed to give orders and exercise control and whoever that person happens to be is also in command. I will now, briefly, reflect upon several important points raised by the final brief of the Prosecutor, such as 36 saying that each Motorised Battalion of the Guards Motorised Brigade numbered an average 700 people. This is simply inaccurate, simply because the Motorised Battalion was the first to march into Vukovar with 428 people. When in item 41 they say that Radic was the commander of the 3rd Assault Group, just one example. I'll use just one example to prove that that is simply not true. P-022, on page 5000/18, when he speaks about Jankovic, he says the following, "His son's name was Miroslav. He was Miroljub's deputy. When Miroljub was wounded, Major Tesic appointed him to be in charge of the Territorial Defence unit along the axis of our company. There are three things that are important here, there is this appointment by Tesic, not by Radic, at the head of any assault group whatsoever. Right, they are being led by Miroslav Jankovic of the TO, not by Radic. And, thirdly, they are along the axis of operations of our company, along the axis of that company, but not actually as part of that company, not absorbed by the company." At 46 the OTP claims that Radic had a command post. There was no such thing. We know that. There was an observation post. And there's a huge distinction in terms of their structure between a command post and observation post; these are two different concepts. Thirdly, company commander commands his company from a combat disposition and the observation post is always where the company commander is. There's also a place where he rests, it's called observation post. Therefore, there can be no such thing as a command post. All can be or, rather, it can only exist, such a thing as command post, from battalion level up. At 54 of their final brief, the OTP claims that the assault detachments were established on the 15th of October, 1991, and that they were reinforced with units of the Vukovar TO. That's not true. That's what they say. The first attachment ever of the TO Petrova Gora Detachment to the Assault Detachment 1 occurred on the 29th of October 1991. Secondly, by using the previous analogy, it is simply incorrect that Radic was in command of the 3rd Assault Group or that it included Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora. Thirdly, this is item 54 in the final brief. It doesn't mean that operations group south was responsible for any logistics support to the TO -- to the Vukovar TO Detachment because it was already enjoying such support as pointed out earlier. There is the order "strictly confidential" 235-1 by OG South for an extension of the attack against Vukovar dated the 29th of October, 1991, and we're fully familiar with it by now. It says, the Leva Supoderica, Petrova Gora detachments were among the forces included in JOD 1, full stop. But it was Tesic and not Radic who was in charge of JOD 1 and that's the essence of it. Item 55. The OTP claims that Witness Vuga is right when he says some important things about resubordination. In order to have resubordination, you need to have a written order. We do accept that to be a fact. I would like the OTP now to produce, for my benefit, a written order on the resubordination of the Vukovar TO and Leva Supoderica to Radic's 3rd Company. Can they please do that for me. There is no such thing; it doesn't exist, therefore, this act of resubordination never took place. Item 55 makes reference to Colonel Trifunovic. Makes reference to a lot of things really, but the OTP are trying to avoid saying what Trifunovic said before this Chamber, namely, that Borovoje Tesic and Borovoje Tesic alone was in charge of Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora. Tesic reported to him and that's how they were recorded in the war log. He reported to him and he submitted reports to him on behalf of the TO and Leva Supoderica not Radic. At 55, the only thing that can be true is the very last sentence about the earliest resubordination of Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora but by the Guards Motorised Brigade and towards other units. That's what I'm saying by the Guards Motorised Brigade and not some other unit and especially not by Radic. That's what it says. Radic's commander was Tesic, item 56. Mrksic enabled Radic to exercise command. Mrksic never made a decision in relation to Radic directly, never. He never gave any orders to Radic whatsoever, nor did he exercise any control over Radic. He was not a -- he was not under Mrksic; he was under Tesic. At 55B, the OTP claims that Mrksic appointed Miroljub Vujevic as Vukovar TO commander. If we accept that logic, it seems quite ambiguous then who the Vukovar TO could have been subordinated to. Item 61. They arbitrarily claim that Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora were subordinated to Radic. If this started at the latest, why the 15th of October, 1991 and it was not concluded by the 21st of November, 1991. That's what the Prosecutor claims. This is an absolute untruth. We have the decision of the commander of OG South dated the 15th of October, 1991, which shows that the Leva Supoderica Detachment is a neighbour of the 1st Motorised Battalion, the Leva Supoderica Detachment. There's no reference to it whatsoever. On the other hand, there is nothing in writing such as I spoke about a while ago, something that the OTP would like to see, nothing on paper to show that they were subordinated to Radic. Particularly erroneous is the statement that Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora were subordinated to Radic. This error is made particularly in item 63 in a bid to introduce what Radic himself stated in that interview. Radic could have been boasting for example. I explained the statement. I explained what Vukosavljevic statement was about those 400 persons. But if they believe Radic's interview, why do the OTP refuse to leave Radic at this trial, when he says he was not the commander of Leva Supoderica or Petrova Gora. Thirdly, and most importantly, the TO Detachment. The TO Detachment could not have been subordinated to a company commander especially not to detachments like that because a detachment is a much larger unit with more manpower. We can corroborate that by Stijakovic's diary. He says he arrived at Vukovar with 428 soldiers and officers and this is very important. If you count them all up, all those who came with the battalion, the volunteers and the reserve officers, that totals about 500 persons throughout the duration of the Vukovar operation. The fact that this is not about Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora can simply and unequivocally be proved by comparing the diary produced by Stijakovic with the war diary war log of the Guards Motorised Brigade; namely, the greatest number of volunteers and reservists who were mobilised drafted into the 1st Motorised Battalion came between the 26th and the 29th of October, 1991, which is consistent with the war diary or war log kept by OG South. This detachment, therefore, was attached to JOD 1 to Tesic, not to Radic. As for the interview, lest I forget, I think it's important for me to point out what the headline is over that interview. The principal headline is, "I am sick of war." That is Miroslav Radic's view. There's that one sentence that the OTP's theory has been resolving around for a year or more. We haven't been able to check it. Even if it had been checked, I explained about why 500 people and what it meant. Radic goes on to say that all conflicts should be resolved in a peaceful way and that he's sick of war and that he wants peace and that is why he was the only officer who is active in Vukovar who left the army back in 1992. That's how he feels about the war, that's how he feels about the crimes. That is something that this Trial Chamber needs to accept and bear in mind when trying to assess the interview. I think all other written evidence is far more important than this single interview and a sentence entirely torn out of context. The responsibility or the command climate, again, a misinterpretation by the OTP. Radic was disciplined, he was responsible. It is strange indeed that the OTP talks about those three soldiers, item 65, that Radic was in command of, as they say, by corroborating the fact that Radic was in command of Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora, but refusing at the same time to lend credence to Stijakovic, Tesic's deputy or Trifunovic. Stijakovic. But also the company commanders Vuckovic and Zirojevic unequivocally stated that assignments were given to company commanders by -- were handed out to company commanders by Tesic and to TO commanders as well. Those were handed out by Tesic, too, to Jaksic first and then later to Vujovic. Is this something that Jakic told us. When we were at the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion, special assignments were handed out to company commanders. We got our own assignments, but I exercised command over my own company commanders because the Territorial Defence and those four that I mentioned. At 67 of their final brief, the Prosecutor is trying to show how they're really familiar with the doctrine. They think they know the doctrine behind the armed forces of the SFRY, the principles of command and control. And they say that on the 29th of October, 1991, this doctrine was to the effect that all forces operating in the same area were to be subordinated to one and the same commander, to a single commander. I would like to read more slowly, but I don't have the time. This is beyond dispute. The commander of the Vukovar operation was Mrksic, the commander of OG South. In the sector of the first JOD, it was Tesic. It is in this context that the position should be interpreted against that kind of background. At 68, the OTP claims that Radic was in command of all units along his axis of operations. That's quite correct. All of his own units and he was coordinating this operation with other units of the TO but he was not in command. At 71 of their final brief, the OTP says that Radic admitted that he was the only officer who had completed the military academy. He assumed the duty and responsibility of planning combat operations. A company is not the level at which combat operations are planned. Planning operations is the highest military level. This is done at an operative and strategic level. Radic may have drawn some sketches and diagrams, coordinated signals and -- and general activities, this wasn't tantamount to planning operations, nor did he have a command post. There were no regular meetings, no such meetings were held. Radic was never recorded in the war diary. It was the name of the JOD commander that was recorded and so on and so forth. Radic was not in command of the Leva Supoderica and Petrova Gora detachments and the confirmation of this can be found in the diary of the 1st Motorised Battalion by Stijakovic. Secondly, the decisions by Mrksic on the 14th and 16th of November are pretty clear. There is a clear distinction between JOD 1 and the 1st Motorised Battalion. What that distinction implies is other missions, new missions, new activity along different axes. At 83, about Mrksic's order, dated the 14th of November, it is unequivocally clear what JOD 1 means. Mine is the 1st Motorised Battalion. This means an explicit order from the commander of OG South to split up the 1st Motorised Battalion and the remaining forces, the remaining forces being Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica. They were split up on the 14th of November on a permanent basis with permanent effect. On the 18th of November, Vukovar fell and it is not my intention to keep accusing Tesic. I'm not accusing him. I think he's an honourable officer. I think he wouldn't have allowed anything at all to happen at Ovcara, but on the 18th of November, he had de jure and de facto control which could have ceased on the 18th of November when the need ceased for an Assault Detachment to exist. But if on the 21st of November the Vukovar TO was resubordinated, couldn't that have been resubordinated by Radic and the 18th Kragujevac Brigade. It could only have been JOD 1. This is a fact proven beyond reasonable doubt. Miroslav Radic, supported by such witnesses as Stijakovic and Trifunovic, is a person who was in no way involved in commanding and controlling the TO units or Leva Supoderica. I see that I have three minutes left. Five minutes. Domazet took a bit longer than he was supposed to, so if I may, I would like to have another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Yesterday, we went on until 7 past 7.00 so I give you five more minutes. Equality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radic's awareness of the situation at Ovcara. He sent two soldiers who reported to him, but not on time. They are right on time and so the Prosecution claims that he was quite aware that they would commit crimes. This is also mentioned in respect of the statements of this witnesses and their credibility as regards his subsequent knowledge of what happened at Ovcara. I believe that we have more than cogently shown here that the OTP had a chance to say whether those three soldiers had indeed been at Ovcara. As regards one of these witnesses, I have shown what was wrong as far as he is concerned. One of the witnesses did and one of them was in the hands of the OTP. Lieutenant Hadzic gave an interview to the OTP. He did not say that he had been at Ovcara and why did not the OTP call him as a witness so that we could hear the relevance of what is claimed by a witness who earlier invoked two dead witnesses and later a live one whom the OTP failed to call before this court? Then we would be able to verify those facts about the three soldiers. As regards the alibi, I believe the OTP must have known that there was a decision of this Tribunal associated with the witnesses Vuckovic and Zirojevic, when the Chamber established that in the given circumstances the expected statement of the witnesses Zirojevic and Vuckovic stricto senso cannot be qualified as evidence which actually substantiates an alibi in the sense of Article 79(A). At any rate, these two witnesses were very adamant. These are people who, thanks to what Tesic stated in the interview to the OTP, actually found confirmation in their accounts. They didn't know that in an interview that he gave to the OTP Tesic had stated that Vuckovic had told him that he was at a dinner with Radic on the 20th of November. Why was not Tesic called and he was proposed by both the OTP and the Defence of the first accused. So following the principle which was established on that day in the courtroom when colleague Weiner was studying Tesic's statement we also availed ourselves of this right and said that what he stated was that Miroslav Radic was with Miroslav Vuckovic on the 21st -- together on the 20th in the evening. So that is more than an alibi. Whether they talked about it with Tesic on the 21st, they may have, but it doesn't really matter. We did not actually pursue this further because it was not up to us to -- to ask Mrksic's witness whether he had seen or whether he was not telling the truth as regards Mrksic's testimony. Radic did not, says the Prosecutor, prevent the members of the Territorial Defence, if the 80th Motorised Brigade failed to prevent them in the evening on the 20th at 2230, I don't see why it should have been the obligation given all these circumstances of Miroslav Radic to stop them from doing that. The 80th Motorised Brigade could have done that at 2230. Of course Miroslav Radic had had no need or reason to punish Territorial Defence because, by 6.00, they had been resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade. Thank you, Your Honours, for giving me this extra time. I'm not going to pursue this any further. I should like to ask the Tribunal to carefully weigh all this evidence to acquit Miroslav Radic for all counts of the indictment from 1 to 8 for the crimes against humanity and violation of the laws or customs of war because this was an honourable descent man, a man who is the father of two children. His spouse is a justice herself and this is a criterion. I made the choice of -- spouse certainly says something about a man and any penalty would compromise the integrity of his -- of his family. And as I said in the beginning, his attitude towards decency and towards honourableness is such that it really warrants an acquittal on the part of this Tribunal. Thank you. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. I see Mr. Lukic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honours. I should like to ask to be granted another half hour, that is to say, an extra half hour in addition to my normal two hours because -- for the simple reason Mr. Moore spoke about solely about my client for over two hours yesterday, so it would mean a lot to me if that were conceded. And I should like to know the answer now. I would require perhaps an extra 15 minutes, that is to say, perhaps less than two and a half hours, but given the multitude of facts adduced by Mr. Moore in speaking about my client, I believe that it would be useful. And another thing that I should like to mention, Mr. Moore has informally told me that he perhaps might not avail himself of his right to reply so that perhaps we may be able to finish, if there is no such reply on his part, we might be able to finish within the allotted time tomorrow. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Can you help us with that Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I cannot possibly give any undertaking until I hear the argument. All I would ask the Court to bear in mind is that we had a significant amount of material which we ourselves did not use and we stuck to our own timetable. The points that we have referred to are in the brief of my learned friend and were in our brief. JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Lukic, we have a heavy agenda for tomorrow because, not only do we have your final brief, but we also have the wish of the accused to address the Court. We also have this question that I submitted to you for your submissions, so I think it's going to be very difficult to -- to accept what you propose. So I suggest that we stick to the calendar that we had planned originally. So on this, we will adjourn and we will reconvene tomorrow at a quarter past.
